speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege to bring to the Speaker's attention a matter which I consider to be a serious contempt of Parliament. On Thursday last, November 30, the Governor in Council appointed John Bassett as the new chairman of the Security Intelligence Review Committee and also appointed Stewart Mclnnes as a member of that committee. In making those two appointments, the government failed to comply with a direct command of Parliament, in contempt of the authority of Parliament.
Section 34(1) of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act provides as follows:
There is hereby established a committee, to be known as the Security Intelligence Review Committee, consisting of a Chairman and not less than two and not more than four other members, all of whom shall be appointed by the Governor in Council from among members of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada who are not members of the Senate or the House of Commons, after consultation by the Prime Minister of Canada with the Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons and the leader in the House of Commons of each party having at least twelve members in that House.
There was no consultation with the then Leader of the New Democratic Party, the member for Oshawa, and he was of course leader in the House of Commons of a party having at least 12 members in that House. The appointment, I submit was in direct contravention of Section 34 on the facts and evidence I have, a summary of which I will submit to you.
The only communication was a letter from the Prime Minister to the hon. member for Oshawa dated November 28, 1989.1 will read the full letter because it will not
take veiy long and I want to make sure that it is fully in the record. It reads:
Dear Ed,
I am writing concerning the composition of the Security Intelligence Review Committee, whose members' terms expire on November 29, 1989. As you know, section 34(1) of the Act provides that SIRC members shall be appointed by the Governor in Council "after consultation by the Prime Minister of Canada with the Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons of each party having at least twelve seats in that House".
The current Chairman of the Committee, the Honourable Ronald Atkey, has indicated that he wishes to leave the Committee at the end of the current term. I would propose, therefore, to recommend the appointment of Mr. John White Hughes Bassett, Q.C. as Chairman. He is an outstanding Canadian citizen with distinguished military service and a long career of public service to Canada. I would also propose to recommend the Honourable Stewart D. Mclnnes as member, replacing the Honourable Frank McGee, who is also retiring. Both Messrs. Bassett and Mclnnis would be appointed for a three-year term. I would propose to recommend the reappointment of existing members, the Honourable Jean-Jacques Blais, the Honourable Saul Chemiack and the Honourable Paule Gauthier, each for a further term of two years.
And I underline the following, Mr. Speaker:
I would like to know your views on these proposed appointments as I would propose to announce them shortly.
Yours sincerely,
Brian
There was no other communication with Mr. Broad-bent's office other than the delivery of this letter to his office at 3.15 in the afternoon of Thesday, November 28. Of course, as was well known to the government and to the Prime Minister's office, he had left for Winnipeg for the NDP convention. The timing of the debate on Bill C-43 was set with that in mind. The government and, as I say, the Prime Minister's Office were well aware of that.
The letter states at the end, and I repeat:
I would like to know your views on these proposed appointments as I would propose to announce them shortly.
There was no deadline put for a reply and quite properly the office of the member for Oshawa assumed that this would be dealt with on his return from Winnipeg. There was no effort made by the Prime Minister's Office to contact Mr. Broadbent by phone, no effort made to contact Mr. Broadbent in Winnipeg, and certainly there were no views provided by Mr. Broadbent,

If I may, very succinctly, Mr. Speaker, I want to emphasize the relationship of Section 34 to Parliament. This is not a mere breach of the act.
The CSIS Act provided Section 34 in order that Parliament indirectly, through the leaders, could be consulted in this very sensitive appointment. I would add this element. This is not a mere breach of a section of the act by the government that may happen from time to time, but given the structure of SIRC established to oversee CSIS, established by Parliament after consultation with the committees, I say there is a very special relationship, and I would like the Speaker to take that into account.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a few remarks, if I may, to assist Your Honour in coming to a decision as to whether or not there has been a prima facie breach of privilege.
The first submission I would have is that a privilege has to be pertinent to a particular member and surely, if there is any privilege here, it would be the hon. member for Oshawa who would be the aggrieved member. One cannot have a New Democratic Party or an Official Opposition privilege. One can only have a privilege
pertinent to a particular member's privileges. Members can be aggrieved, I admit, in certain circumstances. I have not seen too many but have had lots of suggestions. Surely it has to be the hon. member for Oshawa who raises this point of privilege, if in fact there is one.
Second, the question here is: Was there any consultation? The letter is very clear. It was sent to the Leader of the New Democratic Party. A similar letter was sent to the Leader of the Liberal Party. I have a copy of that, too. The hon. member has read into the record parts of the letter, but the hon. member does not seem to place any emphasis on the fact that it states: "I would like to know your views on these proposed appointments as I would propose to announce them shortly". I point out that this was set up to include members from all political parties in order that there would be a balance there. There is no question that that has been met because there are members from other parties there. My hon. friend seems to claim that there was no consultation.
I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no question of privilege pertinent to the hon. member who has raised it because it does not contemplate consulting with the hon. member for Victoria. It contemplates consulting with the leader of his party. That is the person who would have a privilege if in fact there was one.
I suggest that the Prime Minister has made it very clear when he states: "I would like to know your views on these proposed appointments as I would propose to announce them shortly". I also would suggest that theirs is the only party that feels aggrieved by this. I do not know if the Official Opposition is going to become engaged in this debate or not. We have the proof that the letter was received in Mr. Broadbent's office at 3.15 on the day it was sent. I do not know whether my hon. friend is claiming that Mr. Broadbent did not try to get back to the Prime Minister or not, but clearly the Prime Minister asked for comments, did not get any, and made the announcement.
I suggest that the government and the Prime Minister especially have complied with the law. I suggest if my friend has any difficulty with it he can claim that the appointment is invalid because it does not meet the law,

I suggest that there is absolutely no breach of the hon. member's privileges. I suggest that the government has acted in accordance with the act and that Your Honour should find there is no prima facie case of privilege.

Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding what the Minister of Justice has just said, I think there is in this case a breach of privilege and the hon. member for Victoria was quite correct in raising it.
I want to say at the outset that I do not think it is our place as members of this House, on this question of privilege, to comment on the appointment per se. It is to comment on whether or not the process has been followed as required by the act. I want to make clear that my comments are directed only to that aim.
The hon. member for Victoria quoted quite correctly Section 34 of the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act. The act clearly requires that there be consultation with the Leader of the Opposition.
I want to say that the Minister of Justice has referred to the letter that was sent by the Prime Minister to the Leader of the Opposition. I understand he will now table those letters since he quoted from one of them in the course of his remarks. The letter that was sent to the Leader of the Opposition, although I do not have a copy, I understand was delivered at 3.30 on November 28 to his office and the appointment was made on November 30.
I was not in the House when this act was passed. However, a letter notifying of an intended appointment less than 48 hours before it is made can hardly be termed in my view consultation. It is certainly not within the spirit of the act, and I think the Minister of Justice is well aware of that. He is arguing from a position of weakness in this case trying to defend what in my view is the indefensible.
I could perhaps refer him to another act. There are two other instances of this which, in light of the minister's comments, I think I should draw to the attention of the House. On April 18 of this year in Question Period, in response to a question posed by me, the Deputy Prime

Minister discussing the appointment of a commission to look into the electoral law gave the following answer. He said:
Mr. Speaker, indeed, we have been waiting for the report of the Chief Electoral Officer to look at some of the recommendations that he has brought forth. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with the point made by the government House leader that a question of privilege was not raised by the member of the House whose privileges have allegedly been offended.
I want to suggest that it is not necessary for a question of privilege to be raised by someone who feels personally harmed by the alleged breach of privilege. After all, citation 16 of Beauchesne's states:
Parliamentary privilege is the sum of the peculiar rights enjoyed by each House collectively as a constituent part of the High Court of Parliament, and by Members of each House individually, without which they could not discharge their functions and which exceed those possessed by other bodies or individuals.
It quite often happens that members raise questions of privilege and the argument is accepted without any suggestion being made that the person raising the point of privilege has in some way been offended or harmed by the alleged breach.
An example I want to bring forward is the question of privilege raised by the Leader of the Official Opposition several months ago regarding the advertisements placed in newspapers by the government which conveyed the idea that this House had made a decision on the proposed goods and services tax when nothing of the sort had taken place.
Yes, there are occasions when a question of privilege is raised because of something that has happened or not happened with respect to the member of Parliament raising the point. In general I submit that this does not have to be done and, if the question of privilege raised by the hon. member for Victoria is otherwise valid, the fact
December 4, 1989

that he raised it rather than the member for Oshawa does not undermine his case at all.
Second, I want to say something about the point raised by the Conservative member who has just spoken. As far as I am aware, there were no conversations between the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister with respect to the appointments of members of the Security and Intelligence Review Committee. If he knows differently I would like him to tell the House, but I think that I am in a better position to inform the House on this score than the hon. member.
Where I see a problem is with the form of "consultation" in that the letter in question did not state clearly by which point in time a response had to be given. The letter, as I understand it, spoke only of getting back to the Prime Minister "shortly".
What is that supposed to mean? Is it supposed to mean a response in 24 hours, 48 hours, a week, two weeks, 10 minutes? What is it supposed to mean?
If the Prime Minister felt that he had to get a response within a certain point in time and if the Prime Minister intended to have meaningful consultation, that should have been clearly stated in the letter.
The heckling from the government side shows that they obviously think they have a weak case. They would not be prattling in this way if they thought they had a sound case. They obviously feel very ill at ease. I think they realize that the problem here is the way the government is ignoring not just the words but the spirit or intention of the law calling for consultation.
It may be that in a superficial technical way the sending of the letter with respect to the seeking of views on the appointment of the Security and Intelligence Review Committee may deal with or respond to what the act says.
I think we also have to look at its spirit, its intention. If the government really wanted to obey the law, it would have sent its letter in time to allow sufficient checking, reflection, and conversation, if necessary.
Furthermore, with respect to another aspect of this raised by the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, a letter from the Prime Minister inviting views on the appointment to the new International Human Rights Institute should have gone out well before now. This has

Mr. Speaker, I do have a very short intervention. We want to get on to the business of the House but this, of course, is an important matter.
As the other interveners have indicated, consultation is required on the legislation. I thought it would be useful just to remind ourselves what consultation means. Referring to the Collins' English Dictionary, it defines "consultation" as a process where you confer with someone. "Confer" means that you must hold or take part in a conference together.
Obviously, as has been made clear, the Leader of the New Democratic Party at that time did not enter into consultation. He did not reply. In other words, what the Prime Minister did was notify the Leader of the New Democratic Party of his intentions, which is fine, and as the legislation is very explicit, it would require then a dialogue between two people.
This dialogue has not taken place and as the hon. members speaking before me made aptly clear, 48 hours is hardly an adequate time to arrange an interchange on such an important matter. I simply want to make that intervention.

Very briefly, Mr. Speaker. Thank you very much. I do not challenge the right of the hon. member for Victoria to raise a question of privilege, and I think the Leader of the Official Opposition was absolutely right. But as Speaker of this august assembly, you have a duty to consider the letter, not the intent of the law, unless the letter is not clear. In this case, the letter of the law is very clear. The documents tabled raise the question whether there was any consultation. Perhaps there was not enough time to your taste, but the fact is that the letter of the law was respected.
If the intent of the law was not respected, in that case Mr. Speaker, we must hear it from those directly concerned and not from persons speaking on their behalf. As for the letter of the law, documents were tabled to the effect that Section 34 of the act was observed. That's it. Oh, come on!

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to introduce Bill C-34, legislation for the establishment of the Canadian Centre for Management Development.
This bill embodies those principles stated by the Prime Minister in the announcement of the centre on April 14, 1988, and reflects the government's desire to build upon the tradition of excellence in management that characterizes the Canadian public service.
The centre's mission will be to strengthen the management capacity of the public sector, particularly the senior levels, with a view to improving the quality of government and to enhancing service to the people of Canada.
In accomplishing its mission the centre will co-operate fully with Canada's best in the public, private and academic sectors with a view to complementing, not competing with existing institutions. The centre will strive to become a national centre of excellence in public sector management, teaching and research while reflecting the strong traditions of the Canadian public service.
The objects of the centre, as stated in Bill C-34, focus on these issues critical to ensuring our public sector managers have the capabilities required to manage effectively today and in the future. These objects are: encouraging pride and excellence in the management of
Government Orders
the public service and fostering among public service managers a sense of the purposes, values and traditions of the public service; helping to ensure that managers in the public service have the analytical, creative, advisory, administrative and other managerial skills and knowledge necessary to develop policy, and respond to change and manage government programs and services efficiently and effectively.
Other objects are: attracting through its programs and studies persons of high calibre to the public service and supporting their growth and development as public service sector managers committed to the service of Canada; formulating and providing training, orientation and development programs for managers in the public sector and particularly for senior managers in the public service; studying and conducting research into the theory and practice of the public sector management; encouraging a greater awareness in Canada of issues related to public sector management and the role and functions of government; and involving a broad range of individuals and institutions in the centre's pursuit of excellence in the public administration.
The independence necessary for an institution of this kind is assured in the legislation by the establishment of the centre as a departmental corporation under the direction of a board of governors. The board will be comprised of outstanding representatives from inside and outside the public service with the Clerk of the Privy Council and the Secretary to the Cabinet as chairmen of the board.
It is envisioned that the Canadian Centre for Management Development will be a place where highly motivated senior managers will come together to create and exchange knowledge and to learn from each other from top-flight academics and from the most effective practitioners working in the public and private sectors. As befits a first-class educational institution, the management centre will have the authority to consult widely and develop programs and publish the results of its research and case development activity.
The centre's headquarters will be in the historic De La Salle Academy in downtown Ottawa with a second residential facility in Touraine, Quebec. As a truly national centre it will also offer its courses in existing federal facilities across Canada.

Government Orders
In the current environment of rapid technological change, globalization and fiscal restraint, it is critical that our public sector managers have the capabilities to adapt quickly to these changes while continuing to effectively manage public programs and services. The Centre for Management Development will be a key factor in ensuring that this takes place.
As many members are aware, under Order in Council and Treasury Board authorities granted in the summer of 1988, the management centre has been producing teaching cases, conducting research into important public service management issues and developing and delivering effective programming to numerous senior level groups including federal executives, Governor in Council appointees and Members of Parliament.
While the centre's activities to date have been impressive, there is a need in the longer term to enact legislation which will set out specific objectives against which the centre can be held accountable. There is a need as well for the management centre to be provided with the required intellectual independence as conferred by Bill C-34.
Mr. Speaker, I thank you for this opportunity to introduce legislation which will have an important impact not only on the public sector but also on the quality of service provided to the people of Canada.
The Canadian public service has a long and distinguished tradition of dedicated and highly qualified service. Bill C-34 reflects the government's continued recognition and support of this tradition. I am confident that all members of this House recognize the need for a skilled public service and trust, therefore, that they will be able to support this most important legislation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak to Bill C-34, an act to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development and to amend certains acts in consequence thereof. I am particularly pleased because the proposed legislation embodies a plan that has been on my mind ever since I first entered federal politics in 1972. First I want to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Ottawa West for her kindness in letting me make the speech on second reading. Being the
official public service critic, she would normally have made the speech today, but she felt that I would appreciate this opportunity, and I must say that I appreciate this kindness on her part.
Mr. Speaker, in 1974, two years after I was first elected as the federal member for Ottawa-Vanier, I demonstrated my interest in a national administration school. I felt there was a need, and I have been reading the speeches that I made over the years. I quote:
to provide the public service with a staff that on the basis of its experience, knowledge and skills is able to take on management duties after a democratic recruitment process, resulting in an harmonious marriage of knowledge and experience".
At the time, the plan was that this school or institution would also be open to university graduates who wanted a career in the public service. After many hours of reflection and after consulting the various groups concerned, including unions, private citizens and retired public servants, I made this project the subject of an initial motion under Private Members' Business, tabled in the House on May 6, 1977. On October 31 that same year, I had the privilege of introducing Bill C-304, an act to establish a National Administration School in the National Capital Region, as well as a new motion on the same subject.
In January 1981, I decided to table another motion which was debated in the House. The purpose of this motion was to consider the feasibility of evaluating public service employee training and development programs in order to prepare a comprehensive policy in this respect.
Finally, in 1987 a motion was put on the order paper in my name, followed the year after by a government bill, Bill C-46. The House will recall that Bill C-46 was considered by the House of Commons, passed and subsequently considered by the Senate on second reading. However because of the election in November 1988, the bill died on the order paper, and that is why the government is trying a second time to pass the legislation required to establish this centre.
Mr. Speaker, for me, the bill before the House today represents the culmination of many years of hard work to ensure the development and growth of a public service of which Canada can be proud. Others before me were also aware of the importance of establishing an institution
December 4, 1989

that would provide for more effective management within the federal public service.
A number of commissions have examined this question. The Gordon Commission was asked to examine the administrative structure responsible for personnel; in 1954, the Heeney Commission was appointed to examine relations between the Public Service Commission and Treasury Board. In 1962, the Glassco Commission said it had to conclude that training and development had not, in general, received anything like appropriate attention in the public service.
During the past decade, Mr. Speaker, we had the Lambert report, the Royal Commission of Inquiry on Financial Management and Accountability, and the d'A-vignon Commission, a committee that examined the merit principle and its application and dealt with accountability, effectiveness and efficiency in the federal public service.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-34, an Act to establish the Canadian Centre for Management Development and to amend certain acts in consequence thereof, is merely a logical step, in line with previous attempts to improve the federal public service. The pressures on public servants are reflected in budget cut-backs, contracting out and reductions in government personnel, all of which have made it essential to improve management training and development and support management research and case studies.
Like the private sector, the public sector is going through rapid technological change to which it must learn to adjust.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the centre is to help federal public service managers and executives to acquire the skills they need to manage public programs effectively. Furthermore, it will expand their practical management skills and help them find solutions to current problems. We must help them develop motivation, principles, respect for tradition and a sense of responsibility. We must develop excellence by making Canadians aware of the problems of public administration and persuade various groups, including the private sector, to help improve management in the public sector.
We agree wholeheartedly with the objects of the centre which are to encourage pride and excellence in the management of the public service and to foster among public service managers a sense of the purposes,
Government Orders
values and traditions of the public service. Mr. Speaker, these definitions are contained in Section 4 of the bill, and I would urge Hon. Members to read this section, which lists the objects of the centre. Mr. Speaker, I also agree with the centre's object to encourage managers to hone their skills and update their techniques.
I think it would be appropriate to raise some of the points discussed in the course of previous debates, and since this is the second time the House will examine the principle of the bill, I think it would be interesting for hon. members, since we do not often have a chance to read comments and suggestions made by the senators, who, as I said earlier, had an opportunity to consider Bill C-48- This means we will have an opportunity to benefit from the expertise of the other place, as we say here, in its consideration of a bill that is somewhat similar to Bill C-34.
I may add that a number of questions will be raised in committee about the new administrative structure of the centre. Mr. Speaker, there has been a rather important change, and I was advised of this change by the Deputy Prime Minister in a letter dated July 19. In the third paragraph of his letter, the Minister says the bill retains the characteristics of the previous Bill C-148 but gives the centre the status of a public institution instead of a department. Hon. members will recall that Bill C-34 did the opposite. The minister went on to say that as a public institution, the centre will be administered by a board of directors consisting of directors of private corporations, senior members of the Canadian academic community and general administrators of federal departments.
Mr. Speaker, in committee we will ask about these changes. If they were made to guarantee the institution's independence in managing the intellectual aspects of its business, I think we would like to have this confirmed by the Deputy Prime Minister when the bill is examined in committee. Otherwise, I would like to know why the structure was changed.
Mr. Speaker, regarding accountability to Parliament, the bill contains a proposal that says that within four months after the end of each fiscal year, the centre shall submit a report to the minister responsible and that the report shall be tabled in the House. In committee I will ask about the centre's accountability in this respect. Will

December 4, 1989
Government Orders
Hon. Members have a chance in committee to examine the centre's work and its administration?
Mr. Speaker, we are also concerned about the mechanisms for consultation and involvement of Canadian universities in programs and courses. As you know, for many years here in the National Capital Region and elsewhere, the Public Service of Canada has negotiated course programs with certain universities. I am thinking of specific programs at the University of Ottawa in my riding and at Carleton University in Ottawa. I think that these programs benefited public servants, and perhaps the implication for all these previous programs of co-operation between Canadian universities and federal officials should be studied in committee.
There is the whole issue of equal access to the Centre's programs for all Canadians, with special emphasis on women, native people and the handicapped to ensure that they have an equal opportunity to take these courses and obtain scholarships to pursue their education.
My friend and colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mrs. Catterall), has several questions which she will raise at the appropriate time. Mr. Speaker, we are taking this opportunity on second reading to strengthen the bill because we are convinced that the time is ripe and that the Canadian Centre for Management Development will meet Canadians' expectations by strengthening the federal government's managerial abilities. Definitely, better management will give us better performance and all Canadians will benefit from it.

As far back as 1974, I first proposed in a speech the establishment of a national administrative school for public servants. The Public Service of Canada has undergone tremendous change since then, and I would like to cite a few figures for the record to make the point I am about to state.
From 1965 to 1975 the number of employees in the Public Service of Canada had gone from 140,000 to 273,000, and programs had been adopted by Parliament, it is true. It is also true, Mr. Speaker, that we had gone through a social and health revolution in this country of some sort. Pensions were improved, the Canada Pension Plan came in, a whole lot of administrative challenges
were to be met and the Public Service of Canada increased accordingly.
The Parliament of Canada, indeed this House, had endorsed these programs and expected an efficient public service to put into place these programs which the people of Canada wanted. Nevertheless, the fast growth of the public service combined with important organizational changes at management and staffing levels was followed by the inevitable restraint program of the late 1970s.
Staff reductions and cut-backs had a serious effect on careers in the public service. It also taxed the capacity of adaptation of public servants and it certainly raised justifiable fears. Management theories and practices had to change quickly to adjust to those new circumstances.
History has a tendency to repeat itself. Whereas we had appreciable growth in 1965 to 1975, I looked at the figures for the 1975 to 1985 period and found some growth. In 1975, there were 222,325 public servants, and in 1985 there were 223,173. That is little growth, an increase of less than 848.
I must tell the House that there were also some big changes. Canada Post came into being in 1981. That in itself took 60,000 jobs from the public service. These figures must be read in context. In 1981, when the Crown corporation of Canada Post was created, these public servants were taken out of the global figures of the public service. Therefore, there must be some adjustments made in interpreting these figures.
In 1985, we all know that the present Conservative government announced a 15,000 cut-back in the Public Service of Canada. Figures available today indicate that there were 224,026 public servants in 1984. Today, there are 214,253 public servants as of June, 1989, for a decrease of 9,773.
The effect of staff reductions, staff freezes, privatization, contracting out, a whole lot of new ways of administering the public affairs of this country, create difficult problems for career public servants, for those on whom this government, this Parliament, rely to do many things in terms of delivering the programs which we adopt.
There is a phenomenon called plateauing. I want to address that because I think it is pertinent to these discussions. In this new centre, studies must be undertaken to address the difficult problems faced by public
December 4, 1989

servants, the morale problems, the plateauing problem and others which may come to affect directly the efficiency of our public service.
The plateauing of careers has a serious impact on public servants who suffer tremendously from it. In a book entitled The Plateauing Trap which Judith Batwick published in 1986, she explains the phenomenon. As I understand it, there are two types of plateauing.
There is a structural plateauing. This refers to those whose careers are at a standstill because no further promotion is possible because of staff compressions or cut-backs. These people are cut off from promotions through no fault of their own. They are structurally unable to pursue promotions and greater careers.
The other type of plateauing is what is called the content plateauing. This refers to people who have been possibly long in the job who are looking for challenges. Most of them are bored because the work that they are doing offers no new challenge and they cannot find any stimuli in their professional careers.
This certainly addresses what we call professionals in the public service, those who have either a degree or who do specific work in a field such as medicine, veterinary science, engineering or research and development in terms of chemistry and physics. They find themselves doing monotonous jobs and experiencing no stimuli, no chance of doing something a little more demanding and challenging because there have been some compressions. The institution itself is unable to cope with the morale problems that these people experience.
That is why the centre will address not only the training and development of the public service but will address also some of the difficult problems public servants face when Parliaments and governments reduce or compress the public service and try to get from fewer people more efficiency and more effective programs for the same price.
In creating this new centre, I understand the idea is to integrate those programs presently offered in Touraine, Quebec, with programs at a new campus to be set up at De la Salle Academy on Sussex Drive in my riding. In passing, I must say that I am very proud that it is to be in my riding of Ottawa-Vanier, in the school that I
Government Orders
attended when I was a kid, namely, De la Salle Academy. The intention is to put a campus there which will dispense services not only to the National Capital Region, but to western Canada and to Atlantic Canada. There will be programs available to people residing in those areas, responding to the regional concerns that people have in training and development.
There will be an orientation program for all those appointed to managerial positions in the public service which will be available to them within six months of their appointment. These management skills will be centred around crisis management,
This country of ours, this federation, has particular problems in administration. Federal-provincial relations, dealing with vested interest groups, small and medium sized business management techniques are all things which we must address.
Contraiy to some remarks made in the other place, I do not think we should be competing with universities. I think we must rather expand the management training programs of the public service toward problem solving in the management of the federal Public Service of Canada.
We might see this through small seminars, symposia directed specifically to problems of our federation. I am thinking mostly of the federal-provincial problems arising within a decentralized state like ours.
The regional problems must be addressed and how do we address these problems? By co-ordinating with such established authorities as possibly the Conference Board of Canada and others which could give us advice and be important to the development of good managerial programs.
Language issues and how to improve and how to manage them within established government policies is something particular to the federal government. This is something which this House endorses. This is something on which last year, by adopting a new law, we asked public servants to show expertise, to show understanding, and tell us how to better administer this program, a will of this Parliament, but a job that must be done within the Public Service of Canada. How do we address it?
The private sector does not have that same challenge in dealing with regional requirements and official languages. The country has two official languages. There-

December 4, 1989
Government Orders
fore, we must address those problems on a managerial basis.
As I said before, the Centre for Management Studies will also do research in new management techniques in the public sector, to deal with the morale of our troops in the public service, if I might use that word, and the productivity and the efficiency of the public servants and their careers. They are entitled to want to make a career of serving Canada.
God knows we have had an efficient and very effective public service. We are very proud when we speak about the quality of public servants in Canada. From my experience, when I have spoken to foreigners who have come here to look at how we manage this country, they are always very impressed with the quality of public service that we have established.
There is also a need to give opportunities to senior managers and, I would say, those who want to bring forth new ideas and encourage diversity and initiatives that are stimulating to others. There will be a publishing centre in this new Canadian Centre for Management Studies. It will be an experience for public servants who will find themselves encouraged to present papers on their experience allowing, therefore, public service managers to get critical recognition in the field of public administration, not only by their peers, but maybe and more important, by the private sector which sometimes does not understand the challenges and difficulties faced by public administrators.
It is with pride and, I admit, with some sense of accomplishment that I thank the government for picking up on this idea, which has been with us for some time, to give the public servants of Canada access to a centre of excellence where, I would hope, we will develop these new techniques and new methods of public administration.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on access to the Canadian Centre for Management Development, access for all Canadians, not an elite club for friends of the system but a real Canadian management centre where representatives of all groups and regions of this country will be found, which will include women, native
people and the physically disabled so they can benefit from the experience.
Mr. Speaker, this Canadian Centre for Management Development must not become a centre for the Establishment. This country's Constitution states that English and French are the two official languages of Canada. Equal opportunity for training grants will have to be ensured so that all can have access to this high-quality training.
The centre will have to present programs of study, courses and symposiums in both official languages. I am hopeful, Mr. Speaker, that the centre will take this duty seriously.
Mr. Speaker, I do not need to go over the proportional representation of various groups within the Public Service. We all know the record. We know that women are under-represented. We know that we have a long way to go to represent native people and the disabled fairly. We know that employment equity is a challenge for us and, Mr. Speaker, I am sure that we will come back to it in committee when we give the bill clause-by-clause consideration.
Mr. Speaker, I can only agree with the setting up of a Canadian Centre for Management Development. I think that it is a good idea, the time is right, as I was saying, and I call on my colleagues in the House to support this bill, as I will.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on Bill C-34 which passed in almost exactly the same form in August 1988 as Bill C-148. We support the basic principles of the bill, but we have a few concerns about the process which we will be questioning when the bill comes before the legislative committee.
It is basically a sound idea, and we should give the member for Ottawa-Vanier a considerable amount of credit for the thinking behind this because he presented his original bill in 1977 which I believe suggested this kind of an institution.
The parliamentary secretary misled the public somewhat in his presentation of the bill because he indicated or seemed to indicate that this was a marginal start for an institution that is already a full-blown institution and has been in place for a considerable time already. It has
