within the PMO five people responsible to Mr. Manion plus approximately another 100 people who operate as part of the Crown corporation that is to be established as the Centre for Management Development. As an educator I recognize the need for training and the need for research, so we will support this particular approach.
It is very interesting, as was pointed out by the member for Ottawa-Vanier, that the history of the need for such an institution as this has been pointed to for many years. In 1962 the Glassco commission recommended a very specific statement: "Let managers manage". It suggested that there was a need to move away from the flat system that had developed in the federal civil service at that time.
In 1975 the then Auditor General warned in his report that parliamentarians had lost financial control of government expenditures. I can list a number of other items which could be registered as recognition of the need for management studies and a Centre for Management Development: the Lambert commission of 1979, the establishment of the PMS system under the government of the present Secretary of State for External Affairs, and the 1980 value for money auditing which was a direct result of the need to be accountable for the kind of management that was going on.
In 1983 the Auditor General listed a number of constraints in the structure of government which were against good management in government and pointed out that there was a need for better recognition and better movement of managers through the system.
The Nielsen task force on government cut-backs makes this particular approach a bit suspect because we know that the aim of that task force was to a great extent the reduction of the civil service. That particular task force report suggested that some kind of a management structure be put into place.
Things have changed over the years. The complexity of government has increased and the need for understanding, study and research has increased along with that complexity.
It is kind of interesting to recognize that this particular management centre, as it is called, is being established pretty much against the basic philosophy of the Conservative Party because it has said on a number of occasions, and even stated categorically on occasion, that it does
Government Orders
not believe in the setting up of Crown corporations to do these kinds of things that the private sector should have the opportunity to do.
The U.S. model has been to allow the private sector to do it. In the United States republic managed education is conducted almost entirely by the private sector. The United States has set up a number of elaborate and up to date institutions, of which the most widely known and probably world recognized is Harvard's Kennedy School of Government. Other countries have also over a period established the same kind of schools, mostly related to the governments themselves, that is under government control, as this particular bill suggests we are to do in Canada.
We have in Canada a large number of universities which have in place schools with public management programs that could contribute a considerable amount. They could in many cases provide the kind of training research outlined as an objective in this particular bill.
One of the questions which the committee should look into is why we are setting up extensive programs in certain areas when we could-and the bill gives the centre this alternative-contract a considerable amount of the program from universities which already have programs in place, thereby increasing the quality of those programs and also increasing the breadth of them.
There is no suggestion in the bill of the cost of this institution. As I pointed out, there are already 100 or so members listed under the Canadian Centre for Management Development. The principle has been in place since about June 1988. A considerable number of courses are in place that have been quite well and widely accepted. In fact they have received a certain amount of raves as far as their quality.
The bill does not state the direction which this centre will take or the size to which it will grow. I think it is something which the committee looking at it should delve into considerably more.
It would be very interesting to know what the cost of this institute has been to date because it grew from April 1988 when it was first announced to a fairly full-blown institution within the government right now, without, I point out, legislative authority to do so.

Government Orders
I guess that is probably an indication of the direction this government has taken in dealing with a number of its development projects. It proceeded without the legislative authority to do so and established the organization the same way as it did a couple of the departments which were set up before the government had the legislative authority to proceed.
We need to know-and these are the kinds of things which we should be asking within the committee-what the costs have been to date, how far the plans have been developed, and exactly what the plans are. Will those plans be available to the committee for study, since we have had a fairly large group in place working on it? Does Section 16 mean it can be done entirely by contract? Can all of the programs be developed by contract? Will that be a major portion of the expenditures?
Mr. Jim Armstrong, vice-principal of the Centre for Management Development, states in an article in Dialogue that we are building an institution and that it has in place a board of directors which I suppose will be authorized by this bill when it is passed. The board of directors includes leaders from universities, business and public service. It would be interesting to know how the board of directors is being paid since there is no legislative authority to do so as yet.
Although we will support this in principle, we want to look very closely at it. We do have a number of concerns, some of which I would like to go over at this time.
One of our concerns is that since we have not had the opportunity of having Mr. Manion or Mr. Armstrong or any of the officers before us, there seems to be no opportunity for the non-management level of the public service to make a contribution or have input into what happens with and what becomes part of this institution.
There seems to be a veiy great opportunity for elitism to develop if this kind of institution is made an integral part of getting into the service and of promotion within the service. Those things should be looked at and discussed as well. There is no doubt that there is a possibility that it will lead to differing treatment between management and the rank and file in the civil service.
I think that as parliamentarians we should look very closely at the possibility of input from public service employees and the professional institute; groups that should have specific and definite interests in the kind of institution which is used and in the process of promotion, although I know this is not necessarily the basic reason for the institute to be in place.
We must also have some concern about the curriculum, the kind of programs that are developed, because of the possibility of it being used as an elitism approach but also because of the possibility of proselytizing particular points of view. I think there is a danger in any school or institution of it being used to proselytize a particular point of view and make it the reason for the operation of that particular institution. I would hope that that is something we do not have to worry about, but it does have to be a concern.
Mind control by research institutions is not unknown in government and is used in parts of the world with which we would not want to be compared in any way.
There has been very little public recognition of the need for this institution, and we consequently know very little about public acceptance of this institution. Perhaps it would be worth while to have before the committee not only members of the public service but also members of the general public, of universities, academics, as well as people who might want to get into the public service.
Another concern I have is that when the Deputy Prime Minister made the announcement shortly after the Prime Minister made his announcement in April 1988, he said that he made the key role of this institution a matter of getting rid of bureaucracy. Mr. Jack Manion, when he was interviewed and discussed the matter, listed a number of concepts which he said we are dealing with and with which we want the manager level of the civil service to be able to deal.
It is very interesting to look at that list of concepts. They are decentralization, deregulation, deburdening and debureaucratization. The concern here is that all these are part of a right wing agenda to make the government less effective in the economy of the country and in the control and regulation of that economy.
December 4, 1989

We in Canada have used Crown corporations, which surprisingly this is, and regulation to a great extent to allow our economy to operate successfully in our particular economic climate. If we are putting in place a government institution which is dealing with this part of government law and structure, we are putting the concepts of a political decision into the process of management rather than allowing the managers to be administrators of organizations already in place that have been accepted by the people.
That is why, although as an educator I have a great deal of respect for the quality of public institutions and the quality of publicly regulated institutions, I am concerned that it might be possible to direct an institution such as this one in such a way that it would be detrimental to the development of the public service itself and to the direction that the country would go.
As much as I would be unlikely to say so, there is a certain amount of comfort in the idea that there is going to be a board of directors which will include academics as well as the private sector.
I have only a couple more remarks to make, Mr. Speaker. I have a continuing concern about a necessity that inputs into the total structure which determines the kind of research that is going to be carried out so that the direction this institution is going to go will not be entirely in the hands of the government of the day. As the member for Ottawa-Vanier suggested, by remaining a Crown corporation within the government we need to look at the accountability of this institution to this Parliament when we have the bill before us at committee.
To a great extent the discussion that has taken place from April 1988 until now has been internal discussion within the civil service, not even within this Parliament. There is a great need to expand this discussion to the public generally and to use it to develop a kind of institution that becomes open to the public much more than has happened in the year or so in which it has been in place.
Our party will support in principle the development of this institution. We have some concerns at which we will want to look while we are in committee.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise on this bill and to follow my
Government Orders
colleague, the hon. member for Ottawa-Vanier, who has been working on this subject for a long time. I also want to mention that I am following another colleague in this House who for nearly two decades represented Ottawa West and public service employees in this region, sometimes in office, sometimes out of office-the hon. Lloyd Francis, former Speaker of the House of Commons.
As critic for public service employment on this side of the House I examined the bill that provides for the legal mandate and the framework for the Canadian Centre for Management Development on the basis of my view of the role and importance of the Public Service in Canada in the building of the nation.
That is not usually the way people think of public bureaucracies. They are not generally regarded as nation builders. Next to politicians they are among the most maligned of species. They are the easy target of every taxpayer who thinks taxes are too high, the brunt of every politician who comes to Ottawa to clean up government. Many consider them malingerers, leeches on the public purse just putting in minimal hours with minimum effort until they can collect a fat pension.
These are not the public service employees I have known all my life-friends, neighbours and family who have worked for the people of Canada with pride, with commitment to the future of their country and with dedication to the concept of service to the public.
This is a young country, barely 122 years old. It is still a vast territory, largely unpopulated, with 80 per cent of its people concentrated in a narrow band along the border with the United States, a thin ribbon between Windsor and Quebec City so insignificant as hardly to be noticeable on the map. The country is still struggling with its identity, its sense of nationhood, and its place in the world.
It is a nation that has been created against all odds of climate and geography by a vision of piecing together and binding in common purpose a diversity of communities and a diversity of people.
Canada was and is not a natural nation but very much a creation of public policy. Its continued development as a nation has depended on a delicate and changing balance between the roles of the public and private sector and an understanding that has pervaded our 122 years of the role of government, the role of public policy, in building the nation. That is one of the reasons this country developed a public service that has been recognized

December 4, 1989
internationally for its excellence, its professionalism, and its impartiality.
There is nothing we do in the House or that the thousands of members who have preceded us in this House have done to set the direction for the future of society. None of that could have been accomplished without the support and commitment of the millions who have formed throughout those generations the Public Service of Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
I regret that I have to intervene. The hon. member will have 14 minutes left in her speech plus 10 minutes for questions and comments when the debate resumes after 3 p.m.
It being one o'clock I do now leave the chair until two o'clock this day.
The House took recess at 1 p.m.

AFTER RECESS

The House resumed at 2 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, I stand today to offer my party's as well as my personal congratulations to the member for Yukon, the new leader-elect of the federal New Democratic Party.
This weekend every Canadian had reason to smile. For the first time in Canada's history a federal political party elected a woman as its leader. What this says about Canada is that the mores of the past and the walls of gender disparity are being chipped away.
I might also add that the hon. member is in very good company. All her opponents put up great fights, and all of them deserve hearty congratulations.
The hon. member is now receiving mountains of advice from the pundits and the gurus of the media and elsewhere. My hope is that in the midst of all this she manages to take a well-deserved break to prepare for the battles to come. Congratulations!

Mr. Speaker, the Alberta Medical Association has added its name to the list of those calling for a moratorium on the Alberta-Pacific pulp mill project in northern Alberta.
The AMA, which speaks for 4,000 physicians, is concerned about the effect of pollution from the project on the health of the area's residents. A spokesperson for the AMA stated that not enough is known about the effects of the organochlorines which will be discharged as industry effluent into the Athabasca River.
The AMA is criticizing the Alberta government for acting irresponsibly, favouring economic growth and development at the expense of the environment and, ultimately, the health of Albertans.
The federal Department of Indian and Northern Affairs has stated that it supports a moratorium on development of these mills as demanded by the native bands who live in the area.
I ask the Minister of the Environment to immediately impose a moratorium on the Alberta-Pacific project until an assurance is given by the company that it will comply with the new federal regulations governing effluent from these pulp mills.

Mr. Speaker, over the past few days the riding of Montmorency-Orleans has been the site of a major international downhill ski competition for the championship in which the best skiers of the world took part, including a half dozen Canadians.
Rushing down the Montmorency slope, the White Circus champions were able to appreciate the quality of Mont Sainte-Anne Park facilities. The outstanding tourism promotion by management was highlighted last Friday during the great annual reception of Quebec's tourist industry.
I congratulate the organizers of this competition, especially Messrs. Raymond Dupont and Pierre Bour-geault of Sports intemationaux du Quebec as well as Mont Sainte-Anne Park Director Claude Beaudoin for the
December 4, 1989

tremendous work they have done with the financial support of several groups, including our government.
In conclusion, I invite Canadian skiers to discover the 50 downhill ski slopes and the 214 kilometres of crosscountry ski trails which make Mont Sainte-Anne the most beautiful ski centre in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Canadian economy is alive and well. That was the message in a report released by the Organization for Economic Development and Co-operation.
In its review of the Canadian economy the European-based think tank praised our government for its initiatives on the Canada-U.S. trade deal, monetary restraint and the goods and services tax.
The report goes on to state that Canada's recent growth has been impressive in terms of creating growth and employment. The Canadian economy has been second only to Japan in terms of growth over the past 18 months and has created more jobs over the past two years than any of the other 24 OECD countries.
Though not always politically popular, the world agrees that this government is taking the tough measures necessary to ensure Canada's future economic well-being. This government should be commended for its leadership in attempting to bring continued prosperity to this country.

Mr. Speaker, despite its claim of being for sustainable development and a clean environment, the Government of Alberta is promoting the overcutting of forests and polluting of rivers. Despite the rhetoric here in Ottawa about sustainable development, Canada's environment minister is silent about the proposed devastation of Alberta's heritage.
It is up to a committed scientist, Dr. Jack Vallentyne, Canadian Chairman of the International Joint Commission's Great Lakes Science Advisory Board, to say that not only should the proposed mill on the Athabasca River be scrapped but a moratorium be imposed on the construction of bleached-kraft pulp mills until more is known about the effects of toxic chemicals found in mill waste water.
If Canada's environment minister wants to live up to his own words, he should urge the Alberta government to scrap the proposed $1.3 billion pulp mill on the Athabasca River. It is an abuse of precious natural resources, and it is not sustainable development.

subtopic: FISCAL COMPENSATION GRANTED TO ISOLATED AND NORTHERN AREAS
FISCAL COMPENSATION GRANTED TO ISOLATED AND NORTHERN AREAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just came back from northern Quebec where I held meetings with the economic spokesmen for the municipalities of Mata-gami, Joutel and Lebel-sur-Quevillon to talk about the Report of the Task Force on Thx Benefits for Northern and Isolated Areas. Task Force Chairman Rene Brunelle attended every meeting. The residents of these communities were not consulted before the report was handed to the Minister of Finance last October 27. Should the Canadian government endorse the recommendations of this report which has raised great concerns in these communities, the situation can only get worse.
Mr. Speaker, the citizens of Matagami, Joutel, Lebel-sur-Quevillon, Chapais and Chibougamau are in the best position in Quebec to define the tax benefits granted for northern isolation. Are the Government of Canada and the Minister of Finance aware of the fact that Canada's economy needs these courageous and permanent northern residents?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for Yukon on her election as leader at the

December 4, 1989
New Democratic Party leadership convention held in Winnipeg this past weekend.
This election is of particular note both to the New Democratic Party and to all Canadians as the hon. member is the first woman in history to become the leader of a Canadian national political party.
It is with regret that we must say goodbye to the hon. member for Oshawa as Leader of the NDP, but I am pleased to welcome the hon. member for Yukon in her new capacity as party leader. So, Mr. Speaker, I pay tribute to both the past and the present Leaders of the New Democratic Party and thank them for their personal contributions to the democratic process.

Mr. Speaker, talks between the PSAC and Treasury Board broke down again last Saturday. This means that over 2,000 Coast Guard workers are still on strike. Included in this group are federal ships crews who provide fisheries patrols for the lobster industry and others who provide ice-breaking services to ports in Atlantic Canada.
The Port of Summerside enjoys the busiest part of its season in the fall and winter months because of potato shipments after the fall harvest. The Chamber of Commerce is quite concerned that a prolonged strike would allow a harbour freeze-up which could result in foreign market loss as well as a further decrease in economic activity. This, in addition to the problems that have already occurred, is something that Summerside can ill afford.
The most contentious issue in this strike is the wage disparity between workers on the east coast and workers on the west coast. It is a flagrant case of discrimination when our east coast workers earn up to $2,500 less for doing the same job.
The government should go back to the bargaining table and negotiate a fair collective agreement to resolve this wage disparity problem, bring this strike to an end, and keep our ports open. It should not be sitting back waiting until it becomes a real crisis situation and then using this as an excuse for introducing back-to-work legislation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as residents in northern Alberta communities are well aware, the task force on northern benefits has released a report recommending the boundary for the northern tax benefit be changed from the 55th parallel to the 57th parallel and 30 degrees.
The proposed change will exclude thousands of Canadians who live in northern and remote areas from a northern tax benefit. This recommendation will remove approximately $16 million from the northern Alberta economy. The boundary change will pit one community benefiting from the tax break against another community barred from it.
I have proposed an alternative to the task force recommendations. I suggest a scaled-down benefit of one-half for communities north of the 55th parallel and south of the 57th and 30 degrees. I urge the Minister of Finance to accept this proposal.

Mr. Speaker, Canadian people were surprised to find out last Friday that the Balmet Corporation in Saint-Jean-sur-Richelieu had shipped hazardous waste from Montreal harbour to Brazil and that a second shipment is expected to leave for France in the next few days. We know that these dangerous goods have caused poisoning in about 20 children as well as contamination of many lands and homes in the Saint-Jean region. As in the case of the PCB shipments which sailed around the world last summer, this government would seem unable to keep hazardous waste produced in Canada from becoming a threat to the environment.
This government keeps promising to make the environment a priority but when it comes to taking real action to ensure a clean environment, nothing is done. Immediate action should be taken to stop the second shipment of Balmet Corporation expected to leave for
December 4, 1989

France in the next few days. We need concrete action now.

Mr. Speaker, since the days of Edward Cornwallis in 1749 Nova Scotia has had many distinguished Lieutenant-Governors.
It has never been an uncommon practice for friends of the government of the day to be appointed to the prestigious vice-regal office. However, as party politics developed during the 19th century, so also did the practice that those who left the partisan wars to represent the Crown at Government House took on with the office a posture and practice of non-partisanship. So the tradition has remained, and rightly so.
Thus the decision recently announced by former Lieutenant Governor Alan Abraham to return to partisan politics as Liberal Party organizer for Halifax is regrettable. It is a decision frowned upon, I am sure, by members on all sides of this House. I urge Mr. Abraham who served with such distinction in the office not to demean the office but to reconsider his decision.
I also call upon the leaders of the Liberal Party of Canada and of Nova Scotia to join me in this request.

Mr. Speaker, in 1984 Canada and the world witnessed the most devastating of famines ever in Ethiopia. Over a million people perished during that particular famine.
Ethiopia is now facing another severe drought and, again, more than one million people are at risk, particularly in the northern areas of Tigray and Eritrea where the government has expelled relief workers as a result of armed conflict with opposition forces.
Canada must work at ensuring that emergency food aid reaches these people. We ask that the Canadian government use our representative at the UN to influence other governments, including those of the Soviet Union and Israel, to pressure the Ethiopian government
to set up safe transportation corridors to facilitate the transport of emergency aid.
We would also like to see our own diplomatic resources in Ethiopia work out an agreement between the government and opposition forces to form these corridors of tranquillity for international relief organizations.

Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago at the federal-provincial First Ministers' Conference I was surprised to hear the Prime Minister and the premiers discussing reform of the Senate. In his new-found forum with the premiers, the Prime Minister has found himself a new title as chairman of the board. In this extra-parliamentary forum only one of the 11 parties is elected to represent the federal interest. So I was shocked to hear the 10 non-federal premiers speaking of undertaking to reform the Senate.
The Senate is a federal institution and not a provincial one. Our premiers are elected to look after provincial institutions and not federal. They have absolutely no business or mandate pre-setting an agenda for reform of our Parliament. If a premier wants to reform a senate, let him create his own in his own province.
This Parliament must be made aware of the dangers in letting provincial politicians pre-set the agenda and attitudes for federal reforms.
In the meantime, I call upon the Prime Minister to place Senate reform on the agenda of this Parliament, this House and the other place, and abandon his predisposition for carrying out reforms in his private club of 11 and stealing from the jurisdiction of this Parliament and from members on both sides of the House.

Mr. Speaker, one week from today the National Agri-food Policy Conference begins in Ottawa. This conference will provide the first public forum for all partners in Canada's food production and marketing areas to discuss policies and programs.

Oral Questions
Agriculture's share of the domestic product is between 2.5 per cent and 3 per cent and employs 4 per cent of the labour force. That proportion rises almost 15 per cent when related machinery, processing, food retailing and service industries are included.
The perception that large scale agri-business is taking over family farms is not a reality according to Statistics Canada figures. Most farm businesses are family oriented. Less than 1 per cent of farms are operated by non-family corporations.
Working closely with provincial agriculture ministers, farm organizations, commodity and consumer groups is an essential part of developing a comprehensive national framework for agri-food policies. This conference is an opportunity for each facet of agriculture to have input into the decisions affecting their industry as we meet the changing markets and challenging opportunities of the 1990s.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to draw to the attention of the House, and in particular to the Minister of Justice, a very serious injustice being done to a young native student who is a law student here at the University of Ottawa.
Mr. Rock Matte had applied for funding under the Department of Justice's Native Program, but was turned down because he did not have a favourable recommendation from the Law Preparation Course for native students in Saskatoon. The problem is that that course is offered in English and Mr. Matte speaks French.
Mr. Matte is saying now: "I am praying a lot and eating little". The minister's representative in the Department of Justice said: "It is unfortunate that the turn of events were just not in Rock's favour. He is in a rough and tough spot". Indeed, he is.
I appeal to the minister to reconsider this matter and to recognize that the Canadian Human Rights Commission has pointed out that our treatment of natives is a national scandal and that a young native person in Canada today has a better chance of going to prison than of going to university.
I call upon the Minister of Justice to look into this matter seriously and to provide the funding that this young native law student so badly needs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for someone representing the government, the acting prime minister of Canada, in the absence of the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister.
In the last few days thousands of Canadians have lost their jobs to the United States. How does the acting prime minister explain that Gerber Baby Foods is closing its Canadian operation, and that from now on all Gerber baby foods for Canadian families will be produced in Michigan? How does he explain that Burlington Carpets has just closed its entire Canadian operation, and from now on all Burlington carpets for Canadian homes will be produced in North Carolina? How does he explain that the Whirlpool Corporation has closed its Canadian operations, and from now on all Whirlpool appliances for Canadian homes and apartments will be produced in Ohio? How does he explain that in the last week some of the largest and best known American multinationals no longer have a single employee in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure that all of us in this House are in agreement that it is unfortunate these people are losing their jobs at a time like this.
We have to realize that we have a dynamic economy. There are jobs that are being created every day and there are jobs that are being lost every day. It is important for us to realize that, first, the bottom line is that there have been a considerable number of new jobs created over the course of the past five years and that will continue on into the future.
Second, my colleague, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, has a number of programs in place to assist those people in order to help them find new opportunities, new jobs to continue on from where they are now, to support the type of programs that these companies have put in place to assist these people to move from one job to the next.

Mr. Speaker, I could suggest to the Minister of Finance what the dynamics are. They are the dynamics we predicted in the last federal election. When there is rationalization of North American business, what is going to be done and is being
December 4, 1989

done now is at the expense of Canadian workers in favour of American plants. That is what has happened.

Mr. Speaker, Pittsburgh Paints and Glass is putting Canadians out of work.
The Ford Company is closing its V-8 engine manufacturing plant, from now on all V-8 engines will be produced in Michigan.
General Electric is closing its specialized equipment plant in Montreal, in the Saint-Denis riding, so that Canadians will have to buy their supplies in the United States.
General Motors is transferring its van production facilities from Canada to the United States.
Can the Minister of Finance tell us why, every time choices have to be made between saving American and Canadian jobs, multinational firms protect American workers? And now Ford, General Electric, Burlington Carpets, General Motors, Whirlpool and Gerber Baby Foods have decided in favour of the United States at the expense of Canadian workers.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion and Minister of State for Science and Technology):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as his former finance critic has said: "Every sparrow that falls from a tree will be blamed on the free trade agreement".
He mentioned the Ford engine plant. Let me quote from The Financial Post of December 1 which states: "The plant is old, CAW President Bob White said, and we were able to work together to give it a longer life than we had expected". Bob White did not blame it on the free trade agreement, and he feels about the free trade agreement the same as the Leader of the Opposition does.
The Leader of the Opposition talked about General Motors. On the same day that General Motors mentioned that in a couple of years "perhaps" its Scarborough plant will no longer be producing vans, Freightliner, a truck manufacturer, said it was starting up a Greenfield plant in southern Ontario. It has an existing facility in North Carolina. Contrary to the predictions of the opposition, it is not going to expand that plant. It is
Oral Questions
opening up a Greenfield plant in southern Ontario employing some 1,200 new people.
The economy is in a dynamic phase. New investments are coming in. Yes, there are mergers occurring and other things happening. That is what happens in a dynamic economy. It is because we have adapted to a dynamic economy that we have had the tremendous economic performance for which the OECD praised Canada just yesterday.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance has yielded to the Minister of Industry. I want to tell him what the dynamics are. The fact is that when choices are made that have to be made between saving Canadian and American jobs multinational firms sacrifice Canadian jobs every time because they know that for the first time in history they are dealing with a government that has not got the guts to stand up to the United States.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the Minister of Industry: Where is that adjustment program to help the thousands of Canadians who have lost their jobs because of the trade deal? Where is that adjustment program to help the thousands of Canadian workers who have lost their employment because this government has sold out to the United States? Where is that massive program of adjustment and retraining that the Prime Minister promised the day after he signed the trade deal, that adjustment program in favour of Canadian workers who would lose their jobs because of the trade deal? Where is that adjustment program?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. Leader of the Opposition should again be a little more careful with the facts. He neglected to acknowledge, for example, that General Motors Diesel is phasing out its Illinois plant and moving it to London, Ontario.
He neglected to mention that because of the drop off in car sales Chrysler is laying off 4,000 employees in the United States-none of their Canadian employees are being laid off. This reduction in work force is occurring in the United States.
Perhaps the hon. Leader of the Opposition should listen to his colleague, the member for LaSalle-Emard, who said on February 14,1989, as reported in The Toronto Star "It makes no sense for us as a party to blame the free trade agreement for every piece of economic up-

December 4, 1989
Oral Questions
heaval that occurs". He should listen to that advice and heed it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology. He talks about the facts. It is a fact that the work that is going to be transferred from the Ford Motor Company engine plant No. 2 in Windsor is going to be transferred to the United States. When he talks about a dynamic phase, it is a phasing out of Canadian jobs from this country to the United States.
I want to ask the minister this. Will he make a commitment right now to get the Ford Motor Company to place in Windsor some of the new production of engines and components it is working on so that at the end of 1990 the 900 jobs will be preserved and the benefit of this will continue to be there for the Windsor and Canadian economies? Will he make the commitment today, right now?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when Ford opened its new engine plants it indicated that the V-8 plant which was old and obsolete would be phased out some time in the future. The union leaders, Bob White and the union local president, Frank McAnally, said: "Quite frankly, we've been pushing the company to make the announcement for the past few months". They have expected it for a few months. It is part of the national evolution of things.
The fact is any reasonable person looking at how Canada has fared vis-a-vis the United States in this current downturn in the automobile industry will recognize, as the Americans surely do and the auto workers do, that in fact we fare very well and that Canadian automobile workers are more productive than those in the United States. Therefore we have not suffered the lay-offs. In fact, we are getting new investment in Canada which they are not getting in the United States.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The president of the Canadian Automobile Workers also said that he wanted to see new production placed in that plant by the end of 1990.
Is the minister going to make a commitment today to get that new production there to preserve those jobs or is he and the Conservative government simply telling the
workers in Windsor and across Canada that they don't give a damn? That is not good enough.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs; Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion; Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member used the word "preserving". We are interested in making sure that Canada can compete in the next century. We are interested in making sure that Canada still remains the best place in North America for manufacturing jobs.
He talks about the free trade agreement. Perhaps he did not see in today's paper the comments by Ted Newell, president of Dupont Canada, who stated that the $28 million expansion of its chemical plant in Maitland is evidence that free trade is working and that more jobs will be generated at Dupont plants across Ontario over the next two years. That is happening in all kinds of industry.
It is good news, so it does not get the front page feature that some of these plant closings get, but it is happening everywhere. The fact of the matter is there are more Canadian jobs being won as a result of the free trade agreement than are being lost.

Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of Fisheries. We have learned that immunity from prosecution has been granted to certain large corporations and individuals by the minister and his department. There is an important principle involved here. Canadians expect fisheries officers and the minister to enforce the laws that are passed by this Parliament.
We know now that that is not the case. Let me quote from a November 15, 1989 federal document from the head of habitat management which states: "The habitat destruction that has taken place has been ignored to a significant degree. We have determined that DFO friendly corporations or parties with provincial permits will enjoy relative immunity from the Fisheries Act while the small guy gets prosecuted".
Will the minister tell this House why he is allowing certain friends of the government to break the law and remain immune from charges?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I heard the hon. member use the phrase "immunity from prosecution". He knows, as do
December 4, 1989

all those who work in co-operation with officials of my department, that no one is immune from prosecution under the Fisheries Act of offences in regard to environmental pollution, water quality or degradation of the habitat.
The member also knows because he and his party and all hon. members, I believe, support the policy for fish habitat management which I introduced three years ago in this House. That policy reads in part as follows: "The department prefers to prevent damage to habitat and avoid losses to the fisheries resource rather than to take court action against offenders after the fact. However, when voluntary compliance fails to produce the desired objective and the Fisheries Act is contravened and the habitat supporting fisheries resources are altered, destroyed or degraded, enforcement officers of the department will carry out effective enforcement action."
Mr. Speaker, I can provide the hon. member with a long list of cases as to instances where this has happened.

Mr. Speaker, I think the Minister of Fisheries is about to learn that what we are talking about here is somewhat more serious than he took the first question.
We have learned that some large corporations are being granted immunity from prosecution for serious violations of the Fisheries Act.
Let me quote again from the minister's own departmental documents: "Despite obvious and very significant violations legitimate cases are in jeopardy or have been stifled". The example, one of many used in the document, is: "Alcan and their contractors, without any approvals, largely destroyed a salmon stream at Kema-no". That is in British Columbia. They largely destroyed a salmon stream. One would think that is the sort of thing about which the Minister of Fisheries would be interested.
Is the minister suggesting to this House that the stifling of what his officials describe as very significant violations is acceptable? If he does not, is he planning to speak to the Solicitor General or to the head of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to see whether the commercial crime squad of the RCMP or perhaps the
Oral Questions
head of the RCM Police himself, might want to look into the the minister's department because I suggest that there is, at the very least, criminal activity going on in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans.
Mr. Speaker That is not an acceptable allegation to make in Question Period, and as a consequence I am going to move on to the next speaker.

Mr. Speaker, on Friday, Abitibi Price shocked the people of Newfoundland by announcing the closure of a portion of its pulp and paper mill in Grand Falls, putting 250 people out of work inside the mill, and hundreds of people out of work permanently outside the mill, the loggers in central Newfoundland. But the company says it is going to build a new pulp and paper mill in Alabama.
Will the Minister of Forestry look into this matter and find out whether or not the company, in announcing the closure of a portion of its plant, has violated the terms and conditions of millions of dollars it has received from this government over the past three or four years, or is this just another benefit of free trade-take all you can get from the Canadian Government and invest the profits in Alabama?

Mr. Speaker, I anticipated the question because I share with my hon. friend the concern of the untimely announcement of a partial closure of an important facility in an area where other economic prospects are more limited than they would be in other parts of the country.
The decision by Abitibi Price is a commercial decision. It is made in line with the necessary rationalization adjustments that have to be made from time to time in accordance with a number of criteria, including international market conditions, the availability of adequate quantities and qualities of fibre, labour markets and those kinds of things.
The fact is that the particular line that has been closed which will reduce the workforce in this particular mill by roughly one-third was built in 1926 and is hardly state of the art, which is required in today's changing international market-places.

December 4, 1989
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, in a public statement made Friday, the company said: "The future viability of pulp and paper mills in Canada rests on their ability to compete in the offshore market".
The company has become the offshore competition. It is building a new pulp and paper mill in the United Kingdom and in Venezuela using the wood from the rain forests of the Amazon, whereas in this country under this government it is closing down operations.
I want to ask the minister, will he now demand a meeting with the board of directors-it should not be too difficult with the number of prominent Conservatives on the board-and say to them: "Look, you have built a world class company here on the backs of Canadian workers and now you are going to sell them down the river, the Amazon River".
Is the government going to stand idly by and watch every pulp and paper company close in this country? You will be beaten to a pulp in the next election if you do.
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, reference was made earlier, at least peripherally, to this particular closure being related to the free trade deal. The company did not announce the building of a new mill in Alabama.
It is another one of these instances where the sparrows are falling out of the sky, except in this particular instance it would almost sound like a whole flock of thunderbirds has crashed. But that is not the case.
The fact is that the Canadian pulp and paper industry, just like every other major industry in this country, does have to be very sensitive to the conditions in the market-places of the world. While my friend and his supporters may think that we can build a wall around our country and ignore the dynamic changes, we have to be competitive and we have to build the very best in facilities in those areas where we have our natural strength and that is obviously what this company is intending to do.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment
and Immigration. Last week, General Electric announced that it was closing its Montreal plant and that 200 jobs, mostly held by women, would be lost. This company has been making a range of electric lights in Montreal for 30 years, and now most of this production will be transferred to Fairfield, Connecticut. Mr. Speaker, what will the government do to prevent this transfer of jobs and why did the government hide these consequences of free trade with the United States?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is any area under this government that is going to do well under free trade, it is Quebec and the region of Montreal.
We are seeing an expansion of jobs in Montreal as we are in other parts of Quebec where the unemployment rate has been improving considerably. The business people there are going to be taking advantage of free trade to continue to build new jobs in Quebec.
In addition, with the labour force strategy, whereby we are going to be in a position to train people better for these new jobs, we are going to see a lot more economic development in Montreal.

Mr. Speaker, the minister is not up to date on the figures. Every week, there is another plant closure in Montreal. Last week it was General Electric with 200 jobs lost. The week before it was Canadian Steel Foundries with 250 jobs lost. Since the beginning of this year, we have had over 80 notices of lay-offs in Montreal involving approximately 7,000 lost jobs, and most were solid full-time jobs.
What is the government going to do about this serious situation? The people of Montreal want action, not rhetoric.

speakerposition: Minister of Employment and Immigration; Minister responsible for the Status of Women
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the people of Montreal recognize that there is a dynamic economy in Montreal right now that is getting better and with free trade it will continue to get better.
If the hon. member would check the numbers on unemployment, he would see, as I do, that the changes in Montreal are very positive ones.
December 4, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I want to pursue with the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans a very serious issue. Reading from a departmental document, it states: "We have determined that the Department of Fisheries and Oceans with friendly corporations will enjoy relative immunity from the Fisheries Act". This is in addition to the years of immunity we have given those mills that have been fortunate to have a continuous discharge and can negotiate and promise while they continue to pollute.
My question to the minister is very straightforward. Was the minister aware that this policy of immunity to certain corporations was policy in his department?

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not only unaware of that, I categorically reject any such insinuation.
In fact, the document to which the hon. member is referring was prepared by a lower level official in my department, widely copied, but not advanced through the system. I did not learn about it until Friday afternoon. While these are the opinions of one official responsible for one region in British Columbia reporting to his area director, the director general, the deputy minister, and the assistant deputy minister, they do not reflect the policy of this government or this department.
In fact, in the period 1986 to 1988, we have laid well over 100 charges with 47 successful prosecutions for offences under the Fisheries Act and fines up to $35,000. It is absolutely improper to suggest any irregularity or unfairness in prosecution and the application of the Fisheries Act.

Mr. Speaker, this is most serious in terms of what the minister is telling us because, again, it is very clear that the minister has to accept responsibility for practices of his department. For example, when the document goes on and states: "Alcan and their contractors, without any approval, largely destroyed a salmon stream at Kemano due to our special relationship with Alcan."
It also states: "Due to authorization and unworkable enforcement arrangements, near total immunity has been given to Yukon placer miners to harmfully alter and pollute Yukon streams. Even when the miners
Oral Questions
cannot meet extremely lax standards no enforcement has taken place in 1988 or 1989, despite numerous violations."
Considering that these are factual statements, that there have been numerous lax standards applied and no enforcement in terms of where that law has been broken, will the minister do the appropriate thing and offer his resignation?

Absolutely not, Mr. Speaker. I have already pointed out that it is the policy of the department to seek remedies to environmental offences. But when there is clear evidence of intent, on the recommendation of the Department of Justice, my officials and the Department of Justice and those of the Department of the Environment bring appropriate charges.
It is absolutely improper, in fact it is probably one person within the department who has frustrations with the system and technical and legal constraints, to draw these conclusions.

The task force on fiscal compensation for isolated and northern areas tabled its report on October 27. Its recommendations are unacceptable for workers in northern Quebec and northern Canada. It is in Canada's

interest to help workers in the north and near north, not only the developing countries.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister and the Deputy Prime Minister, I would like to direct my question to the Acting Prime Minister. It has to do with the conflict of interest code.
As the minister is no doubt aware, Mr. Robert Jarvis, a former Conservative Member of Parliament and the chairman of the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the past five years, has lobbied on behalf of a private developer to the Ontario Minister of Housing.
Can the Acting Prime Minister justify, in any way, the activities of the Tory-appointed boss of Canada's national housing agency, when he is also lobbying the Ontario Minister of Housing for the benefit of a private developer to obtain money for housing which is partially funded by the federal government?

Mr. Speaker, the first public report of this appeared in the paper today. We are currently looking into the matter, trying to ascertain all of the facts that are involved in the situation. As soon as we do, we will certainly advise the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, let me see if I can be a little helpful to the minister. It is quite clear on this issue in Sections 4(d), 7(a), 7(b), and 7(f) of the code. I quote: "Public office holders shall not step out of their official roles to assist private entities or persons in their dealings with the government where this would result in preferential treatment to any person."
What action will this government take to address what most Canadians would call a conflict of interest, and will this government re-evaluate the position of this chairman of Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation?

Mr. Speaker, I know the hon. member is a fair member, as are all members of this House, and will want to make sure that all of the facts are known and that everyone has an opportunity to fully set out those facts. I know that he would want to wait until all the facts are in before he draws any conclusions from the situation himself. Certainly that is my position and that of the government.

Mr. Speaker, this government's blatant disregard for the Speaker's recent ruling is indicated by the announcement that on December 27 this year Revenue Canada intends to start mailing application forms for the credits on the proposed goods and services tax.
My question for the Acting Prime Minister is the following: Why is the Minister of National Revenue sending Canadians application forms for the proposed
December 4, 1989

goods and services tax credit when no legislation on this has been presented to Parliament, let alone approved?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member would listen to the Auditor General's last report, for example, he stated quite categorically that it was the duty of this government, as it is indeed of any other government, that when there is proposed legislation the government begins to prepare for the legislation to come forward and be implemented. This is why the government is moving ahead, consistent with parliamentary precedents, and within the rules and regulations of Treasury Board.
I hear Liberal members saying that we are arrogant. Well, of course, when I say that we are abiding by parliamentary precedents, we are looking at some of the former Liberal precedents that have been set out, such as the hired 4,000 employees prior to the legislation even being tabled. So we are just following what the Auditor General has said and what the rights and obligations of this government are.
I will let you know one other thing, Mr. Speaker, that if we did not prepare for a smooth launch we would be doing a disservice to Canadians and we would then be irresponsible.

Mr. Speaker, the Auditor General has more influence with the government than the Speaker does.
Since the Minister of National Revenue takes Parliament's approval for granted, although no bill has yet been tabled in this House, he is obviously admitting to us that his proposed schedule for implementing the GST is totally unrealistic.

My question is for the Minister of Finance. Has he asked for advice from the Department of Revenue on the lead time required for the implementation of the GST? If not, why not?
Is it not true that his department has been told by Revenue Canada that the GST should not be put in place on January 1, 1991 because of administrative difficulties?
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, the obvious answer to that question is, yes, we have had considerable discussion between the Department of Finance and the Department of National Revenue. The implementation date of January 1, 1991 has been agreed upon between the two.
That is the proposal being put before the House of Commons, and that is the proposal which I believe can be met. It does require, as my colleague has said, a degree of information, a degree of planning, a degree of working with Canadian taxpayers to ensure that we have a smooth launch of this proposed legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to go back to the Minister of Fisheries.
He just told this House that decisions on prosecutions are made by the Department of Justice. I would like to quote from a departmental document regarding the Swift River case where it states: "The Department of Justice says we should charge the Minister of Forests, the officer issuing the cash sale as well as the loggers. The director general of fisheries has ruled that we will not charge the Minister of Forests, so the Department of Justice will not charge the logger. Consequently, we are locked in the embarrassing situation and immunity has been extended to those responsible for the violation."
I would like the minister to explain this situation.

speakeroldname: Hon. Thomas Siddon (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not prepared to explain the detail of any particular situation today.
I have asked the deputy minister of fisheries to inquire into these opinions of one lower level official in the Department of Fisheries-
The head of Habitat.

He is not the head of Habitat, he is a head of the Fraser River unit.
I would like to determine the extent to which these allegations are based on fact before I draw any conclusions about the very serious, and if not factual, improper allegations that have been made.

December 4, 1989
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote again from the document which states that "Alcan and their contractors, without any approval, largely destroyed a salmon stream at Kemano. Due to our special relationship with Alcan, it has been determined that the violation will probably not be prosecuted".
What is this special relationship that provides for immunity from prosecution? Is it political? Is it financial? What is the nature of this special relationship?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member would note the two words, "probably not," showing that there is no specific component to that allegation in terms of actions that may or may not have been taken. There is no special relationship with Alcan. As you and members of this House know there is an agreement between this government, the government of the province and Alcan with respect to the Nechako River and reservoir which has already produced great dividends to the natives of the Cheslatta Band and will produce a number of other benefits to all the people of British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The OECD report notes the efforts by the Bank of Canada to reduce inflation through high interest rates has been appropriate.
As indicated, however, this course of action may lead to a corresponding increase in unemployment levels. Given the fact that a high interest policy traditionally hits harder in the regions of this country which are less able to adjust to economic slowdowns, my question for the Minister of Finance is this: Given that these measures are implemented primarily to cool the over-heated economy of central Canada, what assurances can the minister give to the people of Atlantic Canada that the government is prepared to act to offset the negative impact of this policy in the regions of the country?

Mr. Speaker, this is a report that has been put out by one of the premier international organizations in the world that looks into the performance of economies and government policies.
I want to quote briefly: "In summary, recent Canadian performance with respect to the output growth and employment creation has been impressive and has brought the economy back to full capacity utilization". It goes on to say that "given the importance of preventing a re-acceleration of inflation, the policy action of the Bank of Canada was appropriate".
It is important to realize that wage and price pressures have been developing in all parts of the country. As an example, in the member's own province, the inflation rate, excluding food and energy, has gone from 4.5 per cent to 5.6 per cent over the course of this year. So we do have pressures in all provinces of the country, both in inflation and in wage settlements.
What we have to do is to continue this policy, because if we do not get inflation under control it will be the weaker parts of the country that will suffer the most.
Having said that, we are still very much committed to the operations of organizations like ACOA, the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, to provide for some offset to the impact of higher interest rates in order to support regional development in these parts of the country.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Finance some questions relating to the response he just made dealing with high interest rates. As the minister knows, in the last two years Canadian exports have lost close to $18 billion worth of sales because of the rise of the dollar which is directly related to the interest rate charges by the bank. The current account deficit with the United States has gone from a surplus of $3.4 billion to a deficit of $2.3 billion. That hurts the resource industries of the very regions about which the member just spoke.
I want to ask the minister specifically, if the high interest rate policy forcing up the dollar is destroying the export markets of this country, is he going to sit down with the Governor of the Bank of Canada and ask him to start bringing down the interest rates and the exchange rate so Canadians can start trading again?

Mr. Speaker, I have expected a question like this from the Liberal Party of Canada which simply does not understand the operations of the economy. It is precisely a question like that which demonstrates that the hon. member does not understand
December 4, 1989

what this international organization has been saying about policy in Canada.
We have had broad support and encouragement from this organization, from the International Monetary Fund and from other international observers that if we do not get inflation under control, interest rates will end up being an awful lot higher than they are today.
That is precisely what happened in the 1970s when the Liberal Party was in power and ignored the problem of inflation. The Liberals swept the problem under the carpet. We saw inflation going from about 5.5 per cent in 1976 to 13 per cent in 1981 and interest rates going to 20 or 21 per cent. That led to the worst recession we have had in years in this country.
We on this side of the House are not going to ignore the lessons of the past. We are going to deal with these problems as they occur and avoid the mess that the Liberals got us into in 1981.

This lecture on inflation comes from a minister of finance who is bringing in a tax that is going to force the inflation rate up to 7 per cent. He has no business telling us how to deal with inflation when he is going to bring in a tax that is going to drive Canadian prices out of sight.
I want to ask the minister when is he going to stop listening to international organizations and start listening to Canadians? For example, the furniture makers say that this year alone imports from the United States are up 29 per cent while exports are down 3 per cent.
When is he going to listen to the foundry association which says that it has lost 1,500 jobs in the last eight months alone? It says that it cannot take the trade deal and an 85-cent dollar at the same time. When is he going to start listening to Canadians who are losing their jobs, their incomes, their livelihoods? When will he start listening to what really makes sense?

Mr. Speaker, I listen to people who are in business and who tell me these things. I say to them right back that we are at a position now, as this report from the OECD has said, where we are at full capacity. We have seen the effects of this in
Tributes
price inflation, in wage inflation, and we are seeing it in monetary aggregates. The bank loans are growing at 12 per cent per annum and have been for some time now.
These are all signs that this country's economy must slow down some. If it does not slow down, if we do not see a control of inflation, we are going to get back to the 13 per cent inflation rate we had back in 1981. If the hon. member wants to get back to that-
Cancel your tax.

-why does he not start standing up and saying that he supports the policies of the 1970s and early 1980s of the Liberal Party of Canada that got this country into the worst mess we have seen in 50 years?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Hon. members will know that a few days ago we had to accept the unhappy news of the passing of one of our former colleagues and by arrangement with all parties tributes will be paid.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to pay tribute on behalf of the friends and colleagues of Jim Jepson who was the member of Parliament for London East. He was my friend and my colleague, as he was a friend and colleague of almost everyone who served in the former Parliament.
There were few members of that Parliament who made a more vivid impression than the member for London East. His buoyant good humour, his great one liners, his love of attention, his pride-he did not hide it being a successful businessman-his happy warrior approach to defending God, country and family, his belief that each individual was sacred, were familiar to all those who knew him.
For those of you who did not know him, you may have thought those beliefs might have been just politically convenient. That was not the case. Jim Jepson did not inherit these beliefs from comfortable middle-class London, Ontario. In fact he represented a riding which was as much working class as middle class. It has many new

December 4, 1989
Tributes
Canadians. It is now represented by the Liberal Premier of Ontario.
He did not inherit the beliefs either. He was, 20 years ago, a skeptic and an agnostic about all things spiritual. When he would see an evangelical preacher on TV, he used to say to his dear wife Bev in his own inimitable way: "I think the elevator doesn't always go to the top two floors for those people". But he became converted and he became a very strong defender of his faith and of his country.
Jim, as all of us know, preferred to learn not from books. Although, by the way, he read five psalms every day and a chapter from the book of Proverbs, he liked to learn from people because he loved people. Although I do not think he probably ever read Dostoevsky, he believed with Dostoevsky that a person cannot live without worshipping something. He said to me one day that if you do not worship God, you must worship something else.
Just two weeks ago we were talking about that something else: ideologies, groups, leaders who received sort of divine honours in their time but were later rejected. The object of his worship was of course God. Jim really did follow the Gospels.
This brings me to the point I wanted to make in this House. It is often said that a member of Parliament, when he retires or when he passes away, loved Parliament. Well, I want to share with this House a little secret. Jim achingly missed this place. He loved it because he was gregarious. He loved it-I do not apologize for this-because he was competitive. He loved the competition here. He loved it too because he believed that in this most imperfect of places there was potential for helping Canada to be renewed politically and spiritually.
I believe this is why thousands were at his funeral on Saturday. Our hearts are with him and his family as he is interred today. I believe that all who knew him will treasure his example and his memory.

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I wish to convey our heartfelt sorrow and sense of loss to Mr. Jepson's family: Bev, his wife and Jane, Craig, and Susan, his children.
Jim Jepson was a proud Canadian. He loved his country and its people passionately. As a member of
Parliament between 1984 and 1988 he passionately spoke of this country, its values and its potential. He was a man with deeply held convictions and for that he was respected by members on both sides of the House. He was a man of honesty, integrity and principles, and that is why he fought for the things that he believed in. He believed in the family, in high moral standards and in people.
Just to give an example of the kind of man he was, in a speech that he gave on November 25 he said:
All that is required for evil to triumph is for good men and women
to do nothing.
He was always an optimist and optimistic about this country. That is why we pay tribute to a former parliamentarian. Canada has lost a good son, and London a fine citizen.

Mr. Speaker, God has taken from us one of his most favourite and faithful children with Jim Jepson's passing. He was a man who lived his faith. Those of us who had the good fortune to work with Jim were saddened when we heard the news of his passing. In many ways he contributed much to this place.
Although we disagreed on many items, he was always a man who was willing to sit down, have a cup of coffee and discuss our differences and explain at some length the position that he took on various issues and reasons for them.
He was a very humble man in many respects. He appreciated that we all held different views and yet respected those views. I say he was a very decent man, a very friendly man. One of the first people I encountered after the last election was Jim Jepson, as he walked around introducing himself to various people, looking forward to establishing strong and close working relationships with members from all sides of the House.
We express our deepest sympathy to his wife Bev and his children. We will miss Jim Jepson deeply and for a long time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jake Epp (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as has been mentioned Jim Jepson was elected in 1984. I remember prior to his election speaking to him about his candidacy. One of his concerns was how this place would affect his family. I think for a lot of us those are the kinds of questions we privately ponder as we look at public life.
December 4, 1989

Jim as has been mentioned here was gregarious. Possibly he is enjoying the scene right now as we are speaking about him, not in a partisan way but in the friendly way that he greeted people and met with them so easily.
He was concerned about the public purse and public issues well beyond the ones that he profiled in this House. He had very strong moral views, as has been mentioned. He was convinced that the nation had prosperity and stability if it relied on the roots on which it had been established, primarily in the concepts that were incorporated in our coat of arms. It is from Psalm 72:
He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river to
the ends of the earth.
We will miss his smile and we will miss his friendship. I as an individual will miss the fact that I think he was the only one who was not daunted by anyone who might have certain positions around here. He would pop in at any time no matter who was in the office and drive the staff around the bend because he had to talk to me. That was the kind of person he was, no airs and I appreciated that.
I remember we would go by this place when the buildings of Parliament Hill would be darkened and the flag would be lit up late at night, and he would express what many of us believe. He once said: "Jake, I still do not know how I got here". He was probably expressing that view for a lot of us. And then he would say: "Every time I see that flag on the Peace Tower I still get goose bumps, and I still get goose bumps from the fact that I have been asked to serve here".
Lastly, in respect to Jim, Jim has finished his race and he probably is best reflected in this House by what the writer to the Hebrews said in Chapter 11, in the modem transliteration which says: "And we have a crowd of witnesses who stand here in the grandstands cheering us on". Jim would cheer us on today, to love righteousness, to respect God's word, and to follow the precepts that are written in the cabinet room on the wall: "Love justice, you who are the rulers of the earth".
On behalf of all of us I am sure we want to convey to Bev, to Jane, to Susan, to Craig, and to his former constituents our sorrow and our thanks for his life.
Tributes
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Thmer (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Jim Jepson was one of the most popular members of this House of Commons. He was liked by all of us on this side of the House. We appreciated his forthrightness and his candour. He was a fine gentleman. He had a radiant and buoyant personality that lit up a room.
I used to tease him about his being a bom again Christian, with the convictions that that meant, the fact that he was not afraid to stand up or express his views, either his theological views or his political views. I must say I was closer to his religion than I was to his politics, but in any event he was a man who demanded and received instant respect.
I want to add the condolences of our party. Jim Jepson was an exemplary member of Parliament, a man who always wanted to get here and when he got here served well. When he lost, he took it with distinction and understanding that in a democracy that is the price one pays for public office.
I saw him once or twice after the election. His defeat had not phased him a bit. I want to say to his wife, Beverly, and his family, and to the constituents that he represented, that he was a fine member of Parliament, a credit to this House, a credit to the city of London, the constituency he represented. He is the type of person we need to elect to this House of Commons.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I want to join other members in the House in saying a word of commendation about Jim Jepson.
Jim and I were put together rather early in his political career because of the seating arrangement in the House. I was sitting in the second row of our caucus over here, and he was sitting in the seat right across the aisle from me in the second Conservative row. As a result we became very good friends. We used to sit here and discuss how Question Period should and should not be run, and so on.
I join others who have talked about his deep commitment to his faith. There was no question that Jim Jepson was one of the finest when it came to keeping his religious faith. He was a good father and a good husband. He always talked very lovingly of his wife, Bev. They obviously had a very good relationship together. I can

December 4, 1989
Privilege
also recall being in Washington with him as one of the delegation to the prayer breakfast meeting there. I was shocked the other night when I saw on the television that he had passed away at the age of 47.
I want to join with our colleague from London East who has spoken very well today and others in this House to convey my personal sympathy to Bev, to the members of the family and to his dear mother.

Mr. Speaker, Jim Jepson and I sat on the justice committee and on a number of other committees together. I suppose we probably had our differences of opinion from time to time on a number of issues.
I want to join with my colleagues in the House in paying tribute to Jim. While we did have some very fundamental differences of opinion on issues, he was always a fair and honest man who treated people with dignity and respect.
I want to join in extending condolences to his wife, Bev and to their children. I had the privilege of meeting them as well at a skiing holiday at Sunshine Village when Jim Jepson and Alex Kindy joined me on a couple of runs.
I was shocked and saddened, as were all members of this House who worked with Jim. Again, to his wife and family our deep condolences and respect.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to take but a minute of the House to add my words of condolences to Beverly Jepson. As some members may know, I was a pretty good friend of Jim Jepson. He once told me of his daughter who had been very ill at one time, and how he considered it a miracle that she had come back to life from the state where most experts were considering that she would not live.
Similarly when I heard that he had become gravely ill I sent a message to Beverly hoping that that same kind of miracle would happen again but this time of course to save Jim Jepson's own life.
I was very much an admirer of his religious convictions. I did not share his views on every topic, but I did share his view very profoundly on one topic. Most members will recognize that as being the topic of abortion. As a
matter of fact, when I took the somewhat controversial position I do have, I suppose, I thanked two members of the House for their support and assistance. One of them was the member for York South-Weston and the other one whom I thanked publicly at that time was the then member for London East, Jim Jepson.
I want his family to know how much I appreciated having Jim Jepson around the House of Commons and how much we will all miss him in the future.
