speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, earlier this morning a question of privilege was raised by the hon. member for Victoria with respect to the appointment of the CSIS committee.
I have now had an opportunity to obtain further information on the matter. I thought it might be helpful if I were to point out briefly what had happened at a previous time when these appointments were made. I did not have that information available to me at the time.
The act that was quoted this morning contemplates receiving names from the Official Opposition and the New Democratic Party as to appointments to the committee. On October 2, 1984 the Prime Minister wrote to the Leader of the Opposition and to Mr. Broadbent and sought their views with respect to possible candidates for appointment to a certain committee. I will read it if I may and then table the letter:
Mr. Broadbent,
I am ready to seek your views with respect to possible candidates for appointment to the Security Intelligence Review Committee established by the Canadian Security Intelligence Service Act. As you know, Section 34(1) of the act provides for the establishment of the SIRC whose members shall be appointed by the Governor in Council after consultation with the Prime Minister of Canada, with the Leader

of the Opposition in the House of Commons, and the Leader in the House of Commons of each party having at least 12 seats in the House.
The members of the review committee are to be selected from among members of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada who are not members of the Senate or House of Commons. A list of Privy Council members effective June 30, 1984 is attached for ease of reference.
I would like the review committee to be constituted in the near future and also I would like to receive your suggestions as soon as possible. I am also writing along these lines to Mr. Turner.
It is our understanding that there were no further discussions between the date of that letter and November 29, 1984. On November 29, 1984 the Prime Minister wrote to Mr. Broadbent:
As you will recall, I wrote on October 2, 1984, requesting your views regarding possible candidates for appointment to the Security Review Committee. I understand that you have suggested Mr. Saul Cherniak. I am pleased to accept this suggestion and wish to inform you that the planned members of the review committee will be, in addition to Mr. Cherniak, Mr. Ronald Atkey, Chairman; Frank McGee, Jean-Jacques Blais, and Mile. P. Gauthier.
I expect the committee will be constituted on November 30, 1984.
I thank you for your co-operation in this matter.
The announcement was then made the next day.
I think that my hon. friend has inadvertently misunderstood the reasons for the section in the act, that is to make sure that when nominations come forward from the opposition parties they are in fact satisfactory to the opposition party and that it is not by way of a veto that the constitution process goes through but by way of confirming that the name of that person is satisfactoiy.
This time both Mr. Jean-Jacques Blais and Mr. Cherniak were reappointed and therefore the Prime Minister wrote the letter that was referred to and tabled earlier, in which he had the closing paragraph:
I would like to know your views on these proposed appointments as I would propose to announce them shortly.
I submit that the section is there because this is a very important committee. When it was originally constituted representation was wanted from all three parties. It is by way of confirmation in the name of the party in question, not by way of veto that the clause is there.
Privilege
I submit that the letter was written and it was received in ample time to find out if the hon. Leader of the NDP and the right hon. Leader of the Official Opposition were in agreement with the names of the former appointees going forward. I am prepared to table the two letters that I have now referred to.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make the following comments on the question of privilege. First of all, I am not aware of the details of what happened in 1984.1 was not here or a party to them. I will seek further information on that and, if I have anything to add to what the minister said, I will so advise Your Honour of these you before you make your ruling.
However, I would certainly say that whatever happened in practice in 1984 does not provide you with any assistance as to the legal requirements of the act and in particular on the question of consultation.
The act says that the appointments must be made "in consultation with" the Leader of the New Democratic Party and the Leader of the Official Opposition. There may or may not have been any reply back in 1984. There was no consultation in 1989. There was no communication, either implied or direct, from Mr. Broadbent's office of his views on this appointment. Therefore, the point that I made this morning seems to me unaffected by the additional information provided by the minister.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the minister's intervention, but I think he has misunderstood the point of the remarks that I made this morning and the remarks that the hon. member for Victoria made.
We were not arguing that the opposition has a right of veto of the appointment to be made by the government in this matter. The act does not provide for the consent of the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the third party in the House of Commons. It provides for consultation only. It does not say consent. If it said consent, I would suggest that we have a veto. The minister spoke of a veto and I am not suggesting that, nor did I this morning.
The minister may have misunderstood me. I did not suggest that we in fact had a veto. What I suggested was that the government had an obligation to consult. What I

December 4, 1989
Government Orders
suggest in the strongest possible terms is that sending a letter less than 48 hours before you make the appointment and inviting comments is not consultation. It is not a reasonable time if a letter is to be the chosen method of the government.
The Minister of Justice is a lawyer, as you are, Mr. Speaker. Your Honour knows the rules of the law of contract in terms of making contracts. If the offerer chooses the method of communication he is stuck with that method and he has to give a reasonable time for a reply. The minister knows that a reasonable time for a reply to an offer in contract made on the telephone will be a shorter time than the time required if the offerer chooses to write by letter.
I suggest that the analogy is one that could properly be adopted in dealing with this question of consultation. The requirement here was for consultation with the opposition. The letter was sent at 3.30 on the afternoon of the 28th and on the morning of the 30th the announcement was made that this gentleman had been appointed to the position. I say that is too soon. There was not sufficient time.
The Leader of the Official Opposition and the Leader of the New Democratic Party had fair reason to expect the courtesy of a reasonable time to furnish their opinion to the government. I suggest that reasonable time was not given, and that was the thrust of my remarks. The failure to give that time amounted to a contempt of this House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think there was extensive argument this morning.
The Minister of Justice came into the House and has given further information for my consideration. I have heard from both the hon. member for Victoria on behalf of the New Democratic Party and the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands on behalf of the Official Opposition in reply.
I will, of course, consider the matter further and report back to the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Government House Leader):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege to draw to the attention of the Chair an advertisement that I received this morning
which I think is clearly in violation of House rules and does affect the privileges of members of Parliament.
This particular ad calls for people throughout the House of Commons to purchase Christmas wreaths and to make cheques payable to a private company. Unfortunately, the ad is placed on an individual member's personal stationery. The office phone number that is published is the phone number of that particular member. Very much, Mr. Speaker, I think it is an abuse of the system in that it does use House of Commons stationery and House of Commons phones and I think deserves to be examined. I am quite happy to forward to the Speaker a copy of this particular ad.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I of course will accept the ad. I suggest, though, before I close off this matter-I know that the Parliamentary Secretary would be most prepared to do this-he might discuss with the other side whether any comment is requested or is necessary and perhaps I could be given some indication of those discussions at least by tomorrow.
There is no need to pursue the matter now. I do not know who the member is and it may be that the parliamentary secretary could discuss it with the other side. I will hear further discussion later.

subtopic: NORDION AND THERATRONICS DIVESTITURE AUTHORIZATION ACT

speechtext: The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-13, an act to authorize the divestiture of Nordion International Inc. and Theratronics International Limited, as reported (without amendment) from a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There are four motions in amendment in the name of the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing- Pembroke set down on the Notice Paper for the report stage of Bill C-13, an act to authorize the divestiture of Nordion International Inc. and Theratronics International Limited. I have doubts with regard to the admissibility of Motion No. 1. The intent of the hon. member is to have Nordion International Inc. and Theratronics pay a royalty to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited based on
December 4, 1989

profits exceeding $10,000 each calendar year. The percentage of royalty would be increased as profits increased.
As I understand the bill, the principle is to authorize the divestiture by the government of these two companies. The argument can be made that the hon. member is introducing a new concept but it can be equally argued that he is setting out a term or a condition must be met in the sale. This, for example, is what is being done in subclause (1) of Clause 4.
I will therefore give the hon. member the benefit of the doubt and allow Motion No. 1. It will be debated and voted on separately.

Motions Nos. 2, 3 and 4 are in order. They will be grouped together for debate and the vote on motion No. 2 will also apply to Motions Nos. 3 and 4.1 will now open debate on Motion No. 1.

Motion No. 1
That Bill C-13 be amended by adding immediately after line 19 at
page 2 the following new clause:
"5. There shall be paid to the Crown corporation Atomic Energy of Canada Limited by Nordion and Theratronics an annual royalty on any profits of these corporations that exceed the sum of ten thousand dollars during any calendar year, and Nordion and Theratronics shall pay the Crown corporation an annual royalty as follows:
(a)	on annual profits in excess of ten thousand dollars and up to one million dollars, three per cent;
(b)	on the excess above one million dollars up to five million dollars, five per cent;
(c)	on the excess above five million dollars up to ten million dollars, six per cent; and
(d)	on the excess above ten million dollars, a proportional increase of one per cent for each additional five million dollars."
He said: Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your comments and your fairness.
I want to say at the outset that Bill C-13 which deals with the Nordion and Theratronics divestiture authorization act is a short piece of legislation that authorizes the Canadian Development Investment Corporation to sell any or all of the shares of Nordion International Inc. and
Government Orders
Theratronics International Limited. The provisions of the bill are probably similar to those of other statutes authorizing the sale or privatization of Crown-owned corporations such as the 1988 legislation regarding Eldorado Nuclear Limited, for example.
The reason for Motion No. 1 is that both these companies had been developing within Atomic Energy of Canada's structure since 1952 up until they became Crown corporations just a short time ago and then handed over to the Canadian Development Investment Corporation for sale. For a while prior to 1952 they were part of Eldorado Mining and Refining, so it is fair to say that 45 years of research and development have gone into what we have in these two Crown corporations today.
Nordion really has done a tremendous job in the field of nuclear medicine for the treatment of cancer. Nordion produces isotope products and also deals with industrial irradiation. The isotope products can be found in radio-pharmaceuticals for medical diagnosis and therapy. Isotopes in bulk are used by other companies for radio-pharmaceutical production and, of course, industrial irradiation, cobalt 60 sources for industrial research purposes and irradiators are used to sterilize medical and consumer products.
This type of research has gone a long way, and these two companies are very important in the scheme of things. What can be more important today as we look around us than the years and the public funds that have gone into companies that deal to a very large degree with the treatment of cancer at a time when the public is donating money for research? The country has spent 45 years putting money into Atomic Energy of Canada and Eldorado Mining and Refining Corporation to bring this research in this field to where it is today.
Today, we are selling cobalt therapy units all around the world and are competing very well. Canada produces something like 80 per cent of the world's supply of radioisotopes. I think that is a tremendous accomplishment.
I feel very strongly that Motion No. 1 is an absolute necessity because the government has been telling Atomic Energy of Canada Limited since the finance minister's budget back in 1985 to either make money and pay your way or we are going to close you down. After all

Government Orders
this tremendously productive work in the field of medicine has been done, it is a very cruel way to go.
These two companies are finally profitable. Nordion has been profitable for a long time. Theratronics has done very well. It is in the profit area now and it was making a profit before Theratronics became a Crown corporation. That was proven in the committee stage hearing of this bill.
Elow can we tell Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, which has spent all those years since 1952 supporting this kind of research for both these Crown corporations, that we are going to sell them off and say good day and then turn around and tell the company to finance itself or else?
The reason for my amendment becomes very clear. Why should a royalty not be paid back to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited since over the years the taxpayers' money has gone into this research and brought these two companies to where they are today? That is why I have provided in this amendment that on annual profits in excess of $10,000 and up to $1 million, a 3 per cent royalty would be paid to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, and on the excess above $1 million up to $5 million, the companies would pay 5 per cent of their profit to AECL. On the excess above $5 million up to $10 million, there would be a 6 per cent levy for royalties to the parent company. On the excess above $10 million, there would be a proportional increase of 1 per cent for each additional $5 million.
This is a very, very small part of the companies' profits, and if a Crown corporation such as Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is going to continue doing this kind of research, build out of that parent company very healthy financial corporations of their own and go out and be privatized by government legislation, then surely there is something owing to the people of Canada back through Atomic Energy of Canada Limited so that that research and development can continue.
Who would ever deny that royalties from a profit-making company that makes the cobalt therapy treatment units and related cancer equipment and medical radioisotopes for the treatment of cancer and other refined purposes in the medical field should not be paid to a
parent company instead of setting these companies up and having them make profits on the things that have actually been done by research money produced by the people of Canada over a period of 45 years?
If the parent company is going to continue its operations, how can it do it without help from those profitmaking parts of the company? How can you say to AECL: "Now, you guys pay your bills but we are going to take all your profits away from you"? That is not the way to go.
Here is a tremendous success story in the field of medicine which has unfolded over the years. It has been a tremendous success. I believe the first cobalt therapy unit was first tested in the Royal Victoria Hospital in London, Ontario. Today they are in hospitals all around the world.
My strong feeling on this is that not only should there be a flow of money back into Atomic Energy of Canada Limited today from these companies, but certainly from any other companies that have been given public funds over the years to become successful operations and to contribute to the treatment of very serious diseases. Surely this Canada of ours deserves something back in return.
This is nothing new. You have royalties on books, on publications and on companies. There is absolutely no reason why this motion cannot be accepted.
I can only say that we are asking the people of Canada to pull out their pocketbooks and donate to cancer campaigns across this country to support research and development and then the government is turning around and selling off two profitable Crown corporations that have developed equipment for the treatment of cancer and medical radioisotopes for the treatment of cancer. We are going to say to the companies that buy them: "They are all yours. Now go ahead and make a profit".
The markets are already there in the world. In fact, there is going to be a tremendous increase in the profits of Nordion in the immediate years ahead. These companies are going to make great profits on it. We have set them up with public funds, they are going to pay a price for that company, but nothing beyond that. They have the research done up to date and from now on, I hope, they will do that themselves in a very effective way. We are all looking for that kind of leadership.
December 4, 1989

But there has got to be something left for those scientists and researchers in the parent Crown corporation Atomic Energy of Canada Limited so that they can go ahead and produce some more dynamic discoveries for the treatment of this horrible disease cancer that is taking so many loved ones away from our society today.
I ask the House to support this amendment very strongly. I hope the government will consider it. It is not asking for a great deal of the profits. They are very small percentages. Certainly the government has had a team trying to put a financial plan together for Atomic Energy of Canada for about the last four months or more. What would be better than to give AECL an income from what it and the Canadian taxpayers have produced over the years?
I would hope that the government would look at this amendment very seriously. It is one that has been tossed around among the science community for a long time. I think that its principle does a lot to really support the argument.
I believe my time is about up. I thank you for your patience, and I would ask the House and the government to give very serious consideration to this very important amendment which I am sure will be very well received, not only by the science community of this country, but also by those who are extremely interested in seeing continued the kind of top level, top drawer research and development that has been done and as a result has produced these two very fine Crown corporations.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words on the motion of the hon. member for Renfrew.
Clearly, the two Crown corporations, Nordion and Theratronics, are not well known to Canadians, although the parent company, Atomic Energy of Canada, is very well known and has given us some of the most outstanding research this country has ever produced. The development of the Candu reactor is the most well known portion of it, although the issue of nuclear energy is sometimes controversial.
The kind of work that is done by these two Crown corporations, Nordion and Theratronics, which really were spawned by Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, is not controversial. There is no controversy with regard to
Government Orders
the tremendous research and value they have given to medical treatment in this country with the cobalt bomb, the radioisotopes that are used in medical treatment and so on.
It is of interest that such a large number of establishments have been built around the world by Nordion, processing plants for sterilization of equipment and so on. I am told that there have been 145 radiation processing plants established in the world, 90 of which were built by Nordion and 75 of which Nordion sells cobalt to.
Clearly these companies are very important to Canada. Nordion sells some $90 million worth of sterilization systems a year and Theratronics some $40 million of cobalt therapy machines. Between them, they employ over 700 people.
I think there are two issues at stake here. One is the importance of AECL as an ongoing entity to our country. Clearly, with the greenhouse effect we are going to need more and more nuclear energy in this country to generate electricity. We are expecting a report in the next week or two which will probably catalogue that some eight new nuclear generating plants will have to be built in Ontario during the next 10 or 12 years or less. AECL should be able to have the benefits of these two Crown corporations which it has developed.
The hon. member for Renfrew has put forward, I believe, a very ingenious way in which these companies could be privatized. Some of the millions of dollars that have gone into the research and development could flow back to AECL for the ongoing research which it is doing in nuclear energy and waste management systems for the country. This ongoing problem will require a great deal more research and development in the years ahead.
It does not seem to make sense to sell off all the money-making portions of Crown corporations in a privatization activity. The hon. member has put forward in Motion No. 1 a procedure for royalties to flow back to the Crown corporation, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, which will give to the Crown some return on the tremendous amount of investment that has taken place to pay tribute to the genius of those researchers who have developed this outstanding research and medical technology.

December 4, 1989
Government Orders
I support the hon. member for Renfrew. I think he has hit upon a very useful way in which the medical profession and medical services units around the world using radioisotopes and sterilization equipment will be able to make those funds available to the parent Crown corporation, Atomic Energy of Canada.
We not only have an ongoing need for Atomic Energy of Canada for developing nuclear energy in our country but also for the disposal of nuclear waste and all that complicated research which will take place. It does not make sense that we just sell off all the money-making portions of a company like AECL and leave the less profitable portions.
Clearly Nordion and Theratronics have been the money-makers and have been successful. The idea the hon. member put forward that we try to retain the ownership in Canada is a good idea. The cobalt bomb for the treatment of cancer is synonymous with Canada and Canadian technology and medical research. That idea is one worth considering as well when we move on to those other motions farther down the page with regard to Bill C-13.
I hope, Mr. Speaker, that on the other side of the House we will get support for these several amendments which I think will strengthen the bill and will serve our country well. It will serve AECL well and will give back to the country some of the investment which the taxpayers have put in to this Crown corporation which has developed modem, new, advanced medical technology. Thus, we will be paying back to the Crown some of the funds which have gone into the establishment of this important and worth-while technology.

Mr. Speaker, I too am very pleased to stand here in the House today to speak on the amendments put forward by my colleague, the member for Pembroke with regard to Bill C-13, an act to authorize the divestiture of Nordion International Inc. and Theratronics International Limited.
I know my colleagues have already mentioned the history of both Nordion and Theratronics but I would like to mention it as well. They have been part of a Crown corporation, Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, for a good number of years.
Atomic Energy of Canada Limited was formed in 1952. The history of these two companies began in the early post-war years and they were connected at that time to Eldorado Mining. In the late 1970s, a reorganization of AECL led to the commercial products division being reformed as the Radio Chemical Company and Medical Products Company. In 1987 both companies were profitmaking and in 1988 ownership was transferred to the control of CDIC which, of course, is the Canadian Development Investment Corporation.
Now we have Bill C-13, which is to authorize privatization of these two companies. This is what concerns me. Theratronics is essentially a manufacturing company and Nordion is a high-tech company dealing largely with nuclear materials and, therefore, Canadian control is highly desirable. They are a leading international supplier of nuclear-based products, serving the world's health care industry. The industrial radiation division produces over half of the world's cobalt 60 radiation processing equipment.
Mr. Speaker, you may be wondering why I am briefly giving you this background information on these two companies, but I wish to reaffirm the importance to Canada and to Atomic Energy of Canada Limited of these two companies located in the nearby riding of Lanark-Carleton in the city of Kanata.
Nowhere can I find out the real reason why these companies are being privatized, although it does give reasons as to why they wish to privatize these two profit-making-and I have to stress profit-making-companies. It does give the reason that they will be better able to compete on the international market and will, therefore, make more profit than they are already making, but I guess this is where I have the difficulty with it.
The companies will obviously then be making profit for a private industry rather than for Canada and Canada has invested millions of dollars into these two companies and into AECL. I guess I am bothered about why we should be bothered to sell them in the first place.
Are we really hanging AECL out to dry on this one? It relies to a certain degree on the profits coming from these companies to subsist or to aid AECL in its operations because it is a research and development company.
December 4, 1989

How is it going to be put up for sale? It is said that it will be put out to the public tender process and it will be fair and square. Will these be invited bids or will they be selective? I think there are too many questions that beg answers.
Who is going to sit on the board? Is there a possible conflict? Who are these people? Is there going to be public accountability? These companies were formed with money from the Canadian taxpayers, millions and millions of dollars.
I know the minister responsible for privatization has said that it will provide these companies with the impetus for growth and development and the freedom to pursue new market opportunities. Those are wonderful words. Does this mean that just because a government appears to be committed to privatization, it must move in that direction come hell or high water, without any regard to who it is going to hurt?
I am a partner in a family business that has been fairly successful over the years. We always sell the losers and keep the winners, we do not sell the winners and keep the losers. This is what is being done here, the government is selling the winners, for goodness sake. I think the losers will be the Canadian people and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited.
Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, as per the amendment proposed by my colleague, should share in the profits of these companies. It needs to share in order to allow it to continue.
I look at other Crown corporations that are slowly being sold off. I think of de Havilland and, of course, the DASH-8 aircraft and of how fortunate an American company was to receive this Canadian company that was finally making profits. Look at the profit-making part of VIA Rail which is causing people in Amtrak to wring their hands with glee. I wonder whose buddies are going to benefit from these two companies.
Twenty-five per cent of Nordion cannot be out-ofcountry owned and I think that is a wise move, but what assurance do we have that that same thing will hold true with regard to Theratronics? We are saying that it will be held by the employees. What guarantee do we have that this will always take place?
Government Orders
I support the amendments of my colleague from Pembroke. I hope that the government side of this House will see merit in what he is trying to do. I think we have a responsibility as parliamentarians to ensure Canadians that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited has a share in the profit-making of these companies and we have a responsibility to ensure that Theratronics remains a Canadian-owned company.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity this afternoon to say a few very brief words on Bill C-13, an act to authorize the divestiture of Nordion International Inc. and Theratronics International Limited. I want, in particular, to pay tribute to my distinguished colleague from Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke who has fought very hard in the interests of Canadians, both at the legislative committee and now by proposing these very thoughtful amendments which he is bringing forward in relation to this bill.
The minister across the way, who is sitting very patiently listening to the opposition's contributions to this debate, says that this bill is in the interests of Nordion and Theratronics. Assuming this is accurate, why then did the minister and his colleagues want this bill to be in and out of committee so quickly? What did they have to hide? Why was the committee not given the opportunity to listen to witnesses, experts who wanted to testify?
My colleague from Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke tells me that he wanted people like representatives of the Canadian Cancer Society and others to be able to come to the committee and make a contribution, to explain their views, how they felt about the divestiture. Did they feel that the bill was adequate? Did they feel that the minister should have provided better assurances such as the ones mentioned now in Motion No. 1? What did the Tory majority do? They did what they are known to do best. They rammed the bill through with no witnesses.
The member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke is quite justly upset about this. I am glad and thankful that our member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke is standing up for Canadians on issues like this.
What does the government want to do? It wants to divest itself of these two Crown corporations which are profit-making. My colleague from Nepean has spoken very eloquently about how this government has its priorities all messed up, how it wants to sell those things

December 4, 1989
Government Orders
that are running well and keep those things that are not, which, even using Tory definitions of how to do things- heaven forbid that anyone should ever use those-does not work.
What are the Tories going to do afterwards? We have AECL, of course, which is the parent company, and now they are removing the paying component. What is going to happen to AECL afterwards? I ask that question and I want the minister to stand in this House and express very clearly and in a tangible way in legislation the long-term survival of AECL. That is what my colleague from Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke is concerned with. That is why he wants this amendment passed and that is why he wants a number of other amendments passed. That is why some of us on this side of the House are standing up in the interests of the taxpayers of Canada, of the residents of Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke, who work at AECL, and several others involved with these industries in Kanata and elsewhere.
I know that the minister is in a rush to get this bill through. He may have committed himself to the Prime Minister or the House Leader, or to whomever, that he did not need much House time and this would go smoothly. I am sorry to disappoint him. Well, on second thoughts, I am not really that sony, but I do want to tell the minister that he is just not going to get it quite that quickly.
I am not known to make long speeches-
No, never.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: -and I would not want to take the time of the House, but if I have to I could be convinced that it is necessary to speak on all of these amendments and to encourage colleagues to do so. Perhaps the minister across the way could save a lot of the time of the House and he could encourage his colleagues to vote in favour of good, worthwhile, thoughtful amendments such as the ones proposed by my distinguished colleague from Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: Can we get a second opinion?

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
A member across the way asks if we can get a second opinion. Well, we have had four opinions in a row here from this side of the House on this amendment, but this is not sufficient for the member across the way, so I will have to encourage my colleagues to provide more constructive opinions in favour of this amendment.
Perhaps if 15 or 20 colleagues spoke in favour of this amendment, all of us seconding the very worth while proposition of my colleague from Renfrew-Nipissing- Pembroke, members across the way would consider that to be sufficient opinion.
We have only had four speakers so far speaking in favour of that amendment. The member across the way has invited us to get more opinions to further confirm the fact that this amendment is worthwhile and we are not going to disappoint him. I promise that we are going to have a number of other colleagues provide meaningful and equally constructive comment in favour of the amendment that has been offered to us as Motion No. 1 by my distinguished colleague, the hon. member from Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke.
I would not want to take too much time of the House because I know so many other members want to speak in favour of Motion No. 1 to amend Bill C-13, but I thought that it was absolutely necessary to express to the minister across the way that we on this side of the House do not think much of the strategy of allowing this bill to go to committee for one or two meetings and then to refuse the opportunity to hear any witnesses, save and except two I think, and to pretend that this is a sufficient amount of debate before the Government of Canada divests itself of these paying propositions which are subsidiaries of AECL.
We do not think this is adequate. We think the bill should at least be amended. Preferably, it should go back to committee. Witnesses should be listened to and allowed to provide the contribution that they would have gladly made had we given them the opportunity to do so. But the government was in a rush to get this bill back in to the House at report stage and third reading thinking that perhaps after a few moments of discussion in the House the bill would be completed. Well, it may take a little longer than that.
The next time the government brings the bill forward it should consider allowing a proper number of witnesses to express their views. As a matter of fact, I invite the minister to stand in his place right now and refer the bill back to the committee and have the witnesses make the contributions that they would have made. If he does not want to do that, I guess some of us will have to speak on behalf of the witnesses who could not appear. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today's debate has been a fine example of the schizophrenia of this government when it comes to the role and the responsibility of government.
We started this morning with debate on a bill, the stated purpose of which is to build excellence and pride in the public sector. To do that we are prepared to set up a national centre for management development with a budget of $11.7 million a year while we are closing down the Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, or at least telling that centre it has no more public role to play, and we are quite prepared to turn over the concerns for
Government Orders
the health and safety of Canadians in the workplace to a corporation that can turn a profit, or at least pay its own way.
This bill takes some of the finest examples of excellence, pride, productivity and innovation in the public sector and wants to sell them. We want to sell these things without gaining for Canadians any return on the investment they have made for over 47 years in the success of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the various corporations that have been part of its structure, part of its excellent research history and part of its development of products that are serving the health needs, not only of Canadians but of people around the world.
The last annual report of NSERC identified that one of the most significant things that Canadians have to do for the good of the economy and for the long term prosperity of the country is to seek out those areas in which, by natural attributes of the nation, we have the opportunity to innovate, to create products that not only meet the needs of the world in areas such as the environment, biotechnology, cold regions living and cold regions research but also to create new economic opportunities for Canada.
I cannot think of another area of endeavour that more closely meets that description than the whole area of radiation technology. We have excelled in this area for decades. We have excelled in the development of new products. We have met a crucial human need around the world with our research and with our products in the area of atomic energy. Now we want to divest ourselves of a superb foundation we have built and with which we can create new technologies and new products and continue prospering.
Not only that, but we want to get rid of companies that Canadians working for their government-albeit perhaps somewhat indirectly but working with public funds-have built to a state where they are in fact very attractive to the private sector, companies that, for a number of years now have been funding further research, the development of further technology and products at Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. We want to get rid of something that is doing well, making a profit and assisting us in further establishing a strong, economic niche which, when I hear the dogma from the other side of the House, is what we want to do, we want to

December 4, 1989
Government Orders
invest in those things which are going to let our economy prosper.
What is the sense of getting rid of two companies that are doing exactly that? How are we supporting research and development and laying a strong foundation for further technology, further products and further export markets by divesting ourselves of companies that are producing the revenue to continue that research? At the same time this government has cut the budget of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited by $100 million it is divesting Atomic Energy Canada Limited of being able to fund, with the companies it has developed, its own ongoing research without further draws on the public purse.
If there is ever a place for public policy it is in the area of the development of nuclear technology and nuclear products. As a member of the environment committee I am constantly faced, at hearings we have every week, with the damage the garbage we have dumped into the environment, sometimes decades ago, is now doing to the world that we live in. I am faced with the need to go back and start undoing the damage we have done.
Nuclear technology is one of those newer technologies which we know produces a dangerous by-product from which we do not yet know quite how to protect the world. It is an area in which the need for public policy and public control is very evident. We simply cannot go ahead and produce harmful by-products as we have done in the past only to have them surface in the future for our children and our grandchildren to take care of.
As Canadians we have invested in this and we are now at a point where we are profiting from our investment and reinvesting that profit into the future of our country. It seems to me that a good conservative approach to this, in fact, would be to keep reinvesting those dollars rather than getting rid of something that is producing benefit for all of us and will continue to produce and benefit rather than allow someone else to profit from the risks we have taken and from the dollars we have invested.
I do want to speak for a moment on the process of the bill. This is the third time in a couple of months that I have seen successful attempts by government members to thwart the democratic process, to cut off debate, to cut off a thorough and careful examination of the public interest in matters. This happened with Bill C-16 on which we were hardly into committee when the government members of the committee were moving to limit debate to a matter of only hours on something as important as the establishment of a $3 trillion project, the Canadian space program.
On Bill C-21, a multi-billion dollar program, debate was limited, and now again on Bill C-13 we have the immediate chop. The people who have some expertise, some knowledge, some insight to contribute to our debate on public issues, are not able to come forward. We are not willing, as a House, or certainly as a government, to profit from that expertise and that knowledge.
Just the two matters that have been in the House today show the contradictory nature of this government's approach. The government talks about excellence and pride and innovation in the public sector and then immediately that happens slaps in the face people who have been responsible for that innovation and that excellence, saying, "We are selling off what you have created. We will no longer allow your current work to profit from what you created; and to see your investment reinvested in the future of this country."
Well that is foolish. That is short-sighted and it is wrong. I hope the members on the other side of the House will take the amendments proposed by my hon. colleague seriously and look at how in fact those amendments will be to the benefit of Canada and the benefit of research and development technology in this country and not simply dismiss them out of hand.

Mr. Speaker, I was not going to participate in this debate but I came into the House this afternoon and read the amendment we are now discussing in the name of the hon. member for Renfrew-Nipissing-Pembroke.
I thought that surely the government is agreeing to this amendment. Then I was informed that it was not and I thought this must be a simple error on the part of the Minister of State for Privatization. Because the amendment seems such a sensible one I could not imagine that the minister would disagree with it. The question of the sale of these companies is one that I would have thought the minister would regard as self-evident. He has decided, in his wisdom, to sell the companies. We may have
December 4, 1989

a disagreement, perhaps an ideological one, on this side of the House with that.
But even accepting that it was a sensible decision to sell, the Minister of State for Privatization is a businessman. I assumed that he was an experienced businessman who would have some considerable knowledge of the stock markets and the way they work in Canada. In fact I think it has been suggested that he was a tycoon, Mr. Speaker. I do not know. In any event, he knows that when you are going to sell stocks you wait until a propitious moment. You wait until your company is at its greatest value, when, in the eyes of the investing public, it will have the greatest worth because it is then that the investing public will pay the highest possible price for the shares.
Here we have two companies that the minister wants to sell on the market immediately. He is in a great rush. He wants to get this bill quickly through Parliament so that he can proceed with this public offering. Yet there is some evidence that these companies are now profitable and they are going to become much more profitable in the years ahead.
Surely if the minister had the best interests of Canadians at stake he would wait until the companies had achieved some considerable degree of profitability and then launch them out in a public offering so that he would maximize the dollar return for the Canadian owners of this company, all of us as Canadians. Surely he would want to sell these companies at a moment in then-existence when they would fetch the highest possible dollar return on the investment.
Yet that does not appear to be the minister's attitude. He says, "I really don't care about how much I get for these companies, I want them sold now". I am amazed to hear that kind of argument from the minister because he is the one who is always harping in this House about the deficit.
To hear him complain as we have day after day, month after month, literally whining in this House about how dreadful the deficit is and how it has to be brought down, and for him to now want to sell one of our assets for less than it might fetch in another year when it could do more good in reducing the deficit, is absolutely astounding for me. Yet that seems to be the attitude of the minister.
Government Orders
The Minister of Finance bleats and whines day after day in this House that he never gets any suggestions from the Opposition on how to reduce the deficit. Well, I will give him one right now, free. Hang on to these companies and sell them when they are worth more. Sell them when the value has gone up in the eyes of the investing public, I say to the Minister of State for Privatization. I hope he will convey the message to the Minister of Finance. He is the one who is always whining that we do not make any suggestions on how to lower the deficit. Yet here I am making a suggestion. Why does he not come running down here and say he agrees with me and accept to either postpone the sale or accept this amendment which provides for a return for the taxpayers of Canada?
We have heard from the previous speakers in this debate on this side of the House about how much money the government has invested in these corporations over the years. That money has come from the public Treasury of Canada. These companies are owned by us as taxpayers of Canada. Surely if we have an obligation as Members of Parliament, and I suggest that the obligation is even higher for the ministers of the Crown, to account for the public moneys of Canada and the way they are spent, surely we should be using our very best efforts to get the highest possible return on the investment for Canadians.
Surely one of the ways to do that is to accept this amendment which will provide that on this very significant investment Canadians have made in these companies there will be return in the years to come of moneys that they have put in by way of these royalty payments on the developed patents and so on that these companies have worked out.
Surely that is a reasonable approach to this. I do not understand the minister's reluctance. Does he think it is going to lower the value of the shares, and if so, by how much? Apparently he will not produce any evidence of this. He did not want to have it discussed in committee. The committee hearings were cut short.
I have read some of the transcript. I have it right here on my desk. There was a motion moved in early October by the Conservative members on the committee that the whole matter be reported to the House by October 26.1 have it right here at page 21 of the proceedings of the committee on October 19. If the minister was not there, he had somebody there on his behalf. He knows what

December 4, 1989
Government Orders
went on in the committee. Eie knows that what I am saying is correct. The discussion was cut short so that these embarrassing facts, these possible explanations, could not come to light.
Surely if they had come to light and the Canadian public became aware that by holding on to the shares of these companies for another year, or by agreeing to an amendment such as the one that we are discussing today, the Canadian public would get a greater return on the sale of these assets, the public would have agreed with us that this amendment is entirely suitable and entirely proper.
I say to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, reconsider your decision, Mr. Minister, to reject this amendment. Look at it in a more favourable light. This is doing something for the people of Canada who put their dollars into these corporations over the years. This is getting the money back on these dollars that are being forgone by the immediate sale. If that money can be recovered in this way, surely it is a reasonable way for us as the House of Commons to deal with this bill and say, look, the people of Canada deserve better than a quick fire sale of these corporations. Surely they deserve to get something for the substantial investment that they have put in and that will be coming back over the next few years in sales of the products that these companies manufacture, increase and improve.
That is the evidence we have before us. On the limited evidence that we have that would seem to be the view of the people who are running these corporations. Surely the Minister of State for Privatization has an obligation to speak for these companies, not just to speak for the potential investors who want to snap these shares up at bargain prices, but that seems to be his aim.
This government has rushed headlong into this privatization nonsense. It has sold off assets that belong to the Canadian taxpayers, sold them to a select few of those taxpayers at fire sale prices, I suggest. We should discontinue this practice at once. These companies have significant assets. These companies have invested a great deal of money in developing certain patents and procedures that can be marketed. Surely Canadians should get a return on those developments, those patents and those procedures.
The royalty scheme that is suggested in the amendment by my distinguished colleague from Renfrew-Ni-pissing-Pembroke deserves the consideration of the minister instead of this apparent rejection, disinterest and lack of concern. Surely the minister has an obligation to the people of Canada to speak up and support this amendment, and I invite him to do so.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to start by congratulating the member for Renfrew- Nipissing-Pembroke for his effort to introduce an amendment to this House on a subject that is very dear to my heart. As someone who has been involved in research and development, as well as someone who worked in the private sector for a number of years, I know too well the importance of research and development for our country and for the well-being of our economy.
The amendment put before the House is nothing more than an assurance that the government and Canadians can rely on. Asking an ambassador or someone who is interested in purchasing a company, or a group of people who are planning to purchase a company, to pay a part of the profit to Atomic Energy so that it can be used in research and development is not asking a lot. If anything this money could be put to a proper use. It will be put to proper use by Atomic Energy, a corporation that has over the past decades done a tremendous amount of work in the area of research and development in the advancement of technology in Canada.
I have looked over the four different amendments and to me they make a lot of sense. I would say: why not? Normally when people sell an item it is because they are not satisfied with it. It is a white elephant, an item that is not generating any kind of revenue. They sell something because it is not serving the purpose.
My God, we have two world-class corporations about which every Canadian can be proud-those on the local scene and those on the international scene. We are planning to put them on the market so that we can sell them and so that we can get the funds.
I would say that if the government had been up front and indicated that all of the revenues from the sale of these corporations would go toward research and development, probably I would not have stood up in order to speak on this issue. But in the absence of any kind of
December 4, 1989

assurances that the proceeds from the sale of these two corporations, if and when they are sold, will go toward research and development, I find it alarming for a great many reasons.
First, the Prime Minister himself day after day at every possible opportunity has spoken on the issue of research and development. I have a lot of admiration for everything that he has said so far on this issue. He has spoken on the issue of education. He has spoken on the importance of Canada being competitive in the international market. I appreciate that very much. But now I have seen the government proceeding with the sale of two of the finest corporations owned by Canadians without giving any kind of assurances that the proceeds will go toward research and development. It is quite alarming.
I would suggest to the minister and to the government that it is not too late. We still have some time. Mr. Speaker, I would like first to thank the House for this

opportunity to speak on Bill C-13 and the amendments to it presented by my learned colleague from Renfrew.
First, I think it would be important to talk about the theory and the importance of the Tory ideology as it relates to the selling off of Crown corporations before we get involved in the bill itself. I think it would be important for the people of Canada to understand what we are doing here today as members of Parliament.
It is not so much the fact that we are selling off Crown corporations which is very difficult to stomach; it is the fact that we spend millions and millions of dollars of taxpayers' money to improve on a particular area that is deficient in our country, for example, research and development related to atomic energy. We get involved in that particular process at the taxpayers' expense. Once we get to a certain point in its evolution and its history, this particular government has decided that it is time to give it back to private enterprise. In itself that is not so bad. The situation that is really intolerable is the way it has been done.
First, lengthy debate did not take place before it happened. In reality there has been no debate at all. If the people of Canada knew just what is being given away and what is being put out there on the block and the fact that there is not going to be a lot of benefit to Canadians once it is sold, then I think there would be a large outcry by Canadians as it relates to that issue.
What really makes me nervous about this whole particular ideology is that there are other Crown corporations out there that have not been sold yet which the minister would love to get his hands on to give back to private enterprise. An example of this would be Canada Post. It will not happen just yet since it has not started to create enough of a profit.
That is a perfect example of an issue that in this particular term of this particular government could become a bit of a national debate in the sense that once it becomes a profitable corporation it would be much easier to sell. Therefore, when that takes place, we will be looking at the same type of philosophy that we are seeing now. It is simply this-there is no debate. It is being pushed through as quickly as possible so that Canadians will not realize what is happening. They have so much on their plate now.
We have the GST that is keeping everybody busy. We have the abortion bill about which everybody is in an uproar. Everybody is in such a disturbing state as it relates to the direction this particular government is taking that these lesser areas of emphasis, these smaller

areas of change, may not be as visible and can go through without extensive debate. That in itself is a shame for a country that considers itself to be by far one of the most democratic countries in the world.

Why should this not be an issue for people to stand up and toss around their own ideas on, whether it be on the socialist side, the Liberal side, or the Conservative side?
Let us take a look at another area of major concern as it relates to this bill. I refer to the number of dollars that were pumped into these particular companies. The people of Canada felt that it was a responsible situation for past governments to get involved in. Now they are going to lose that feeling for that particular company because it is going to be put back in the private sector.
That is not so bad if there is a rationale behind it, but the minister and the government are bullying their way through the privatization of many Crown corporations, and we have no understanding as to why. The rationale behind this particular privatization is simply this: these companies will be more competitive in the international market.
I ask this simple question through you, Mr. Speaker, of the minister: If there are problems with marketing on the international scene, why not give that company the opportunity to allow for that change to take place? Therefore we would resolve that situation. Instead of selling off a very competitive company that is paying dividends to the taxpayers of Canada, after so many years of we taxpayers paying into it, here was a perfect opportunity for us to get some money back for a change, but once it becomes profitable this government wants to give it away. I have difficulty understanding the rationale for that.
What is really scary about all this is when we consider what may happen when CN becomes profitable. That should not be too long once it starts selling off everything and once it becomes a little bit more profitable. That may not be in this mandate, but it could be in a few mandates down the road. Maybe it will even make it in
the next three or four years and this particular government will have the opportunity to give it away.
If we take a look at the number of dollars the taxpayers pumped into CN and the roadbeds that go with it, we see that we are talking about billions and billions of dollars. You will never get that back if you sell that company. But, then, does that matter to this particular government?
It is not so much the fact that we sell something that bothers us. It is how it is done and why it is done. That is the issue here. That is what we are debating here. My hon. colleague has put some amendments forward. They are good amendments because they protect the investment of the taxpayers of this country who have invested dearly in these companies.
I would like to ask the minister to stand up in his place and give us his rationale as to why we do not give the taxpayers of Canada some incentive to continue to buy these shares once these companies go on the open market, knowing that the taxpayers of Canada will receive some return.
Who is to say that the people who buy these shares will be Canadians? Who is to say it will not be some foreign investors who come in and buy the shares of this particular company? What will happen is that we will have companies operating in Canada that are owned in part by foreigners.
It is important for Canadians to understand that it is not so bad that a foreigner might buy a few shares of particular Crown corporations. What is drastically disgusting-and I think members opposite should look at this very seriously-is that more and more of the companies in this country are not owned by Canadians but by multinationals or subsidiaries of those multinationals. I think that is something of major importance in this debate. It is something we should look at seriously.
If the minister were serious in enhancing the debate on the privatization of Crown corporations in a more equitable and fulfilling manner for the members in this House, he would allow the committee to review and to ask to hear from a lot more witnesses than have been asked to come forward. nothing which is even worse. If that is the case and if it is acceptable to Canadians, we will agree with the government that that is the way to go.

speechtext:
The rules that we set up for the NDP leadership contest with respect to maximum spending limits, campaign donations, maximum donations are modelled along the lines of the Canada Elections Act.
The reason that the New Democratic Party sets up these rules is so that leadership contests can be conducted on a fair and equal basis between party members who are contesting for leadership, but also so that the people of Canada who are electing probably the most important offices in the House of Commons can have absolute certainty and absolute assurance that these offices are not purchased by people seeking political favours and seeking the right to influence leaders, but people who are governed by the same kind of strict rules that apply to the election of all members under the Canada Elections Act.
We feel that the rules that we have adopted and the rules that apply to Members of Parliament should also apply to members seeking the leadership of their parties. Others would say that political parties are groups that are independent of the House of Commons and that we have absolutely no right to interfere in their operations. As I say, the people who are selected as leaders of these parties will be sitting in the House of Commons leading their parties and also will have the opportunity at some time in the future to lead governments in this country. We should be absolutely clear and certain, and we should
make sure that the people of Canada are absolutely clear and certain that their leaders have not been purchased as a result of people who are able to make large donations, influencing the outcome of leadership conventions.
I recall a national convention a few years back that attracted a lot of play in the media and on television. A lot of stories circulated around that convention about derelicts being purchased off the streets and given convention credentials. You may remember these stories, Mr. Speaker. As a result those derelicts who were not even members of the Conservative Party-I was not going to mention the party-ended up going to the convention with credentials and supporting a particular leader, and they will be available for the next convention to come.
If we have clear and well defined instructions laid down under the Canada Elections Act to restrict the amount of money that is spent by leadership candidates and to require disclosure as to who makes those donations, and also have limits on individual donations, then Canadians can be certain that their leadership is not purchased, but that it is won by democratic means within the existing political parties.
Therefore, I hope that all Members of the House of Commons will support this private member's motion and would back it to the hilt.
As a result of the disclosure requirements at the NDP convention in Winnipeg last week, there was a limit established for our leadership candidates of $150,000. Only one of the leadership candidates spent more than half of that sum. I think the maximum sum spent was $80,000. Most of the front-runners in that leadership campaign spent $30,000 to $40,000, a third of the limit. This is money that they expended in travelling back and forth across Canada to speak to hundreds of constituents and at public meetings across Canada and dealing with the media across Canada, in addition to all the expenses they had in the convention itself.
I have seen other examples of conventions. I will mention one in British Columbia so no one in this House will take offence. The convention in British Columbia was held in a facility owned by a close friend of the front-running leadership candidate. During the convention, that close friend of the front-running leadership candidate also paid the full campaign expenses of the candidates as they dropped off the ballot in order to assure that their votes would go to the front-runner and assure his leadership. That person became the premier of the province without even holding an elected seat in the legislature of British Columbia. His name was Bill
$H|i

Vander Zalm. He is still the premier but he is elected now.
The people of British Columbia got the idea as a result of that convention that the premiership of the province was up for sale and could be purchased by the candidate who had the wealthiest friends, and that is precisely what happened. That kind of thing should not be permitted to happen in Canada. This Parliament should be concerned that we have rules governing the election of leaders in political parties and that those rules are as strictly enforced as are the rules for all members under the Canada Elections Act so that we can be assured as well that the leadership of political parties is not up for sale and is conducted on a free, democratic and fair basis. Basically, all we are asking Parliament to do in this resolution is to make sure that leaderships are free and democratic within the major political parties in Canada.
I was reading the newspapers recently and saw that one candidate for the Liberal leadership was talking about raising $1 million in order to finance her leadership campaign. I will not mention her name, of course. She is not here today, but she was talking about raising $1 million to conduct a leadership campaign.
As I said, the person who spent the most in the NDP leadership campaign spent $80,000 out of a total expenditure limit of $150,000. She used that money to travel across Canada. She used that money to have her campaign workers make phone calls to all of the membership. She used that money to present herself and rent halls at public meetings. She used that money to buy all the necessary signs and trappings of a leadership campaign when it finally gets into the convention, and she only spent $80,000. What is a million dollars going to do? What is a million dollars going to buy that only required $80,000 in the case I just mentioned?
All we are asking is that that money be disclosed as to its source and that money be disclosed as to who donated it and what it was paid out for. We would not like to see money in leadership campaigns used as it has been in the past, to pay derelicts to come off the street and vote for people who may ultimately be the Prime Minister of

Canada, or to pay members of youth groups to suddenly become members of a political party and end up on the floor of the convention voting for leaders.
We want to see this process be as fair, honest, and as straight up as possible. We want to see the people of Canada feel that their leaders have been elected democratically and not purchased by people who have big money and as a result those leaders are beholden to the highest bidders, to the highest donors. That is the reason for this motion. All members recognize that there are deficiencies in the Elections Act and in the expenditure provisions under the Elections Act. It does not cover that period prior to a nomination being obtained when a large amount of money can change hands and there is no real control over how that money changes hands in order to secure nominations.
The same is true of the way money changes hands at leadership conventions in order to purchase the votes of people who will vote at that convention. We want to make sure that it is as honest, as open and as up-front as possible. I hope that all members will support this very well advised private member's motion.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion of my colleague, the member for Comox-Alberni, proposes that the government should consider establishing spending limits and rules of disclosure listing all campaign contributions by source and amount for all Canadian political party leadership races.
Hon. members may recall that the government in its Speech from the Throne on April 3, 1989 announced its intention to appoint a commission of inquiry to make recommendations for needed changes and reforms to the electoral laws. On November 15, 1989 the Prime Minister in fact announced the establishment of such a commission of inquiry to be chaired by Mr. Pierre Lortie. Hon. members will be pleased to note that the terms of reference of the commission extend beyond the principles and process that should govern the election of

December 4, 1989
Private Members' Business
members of the House of Commons to the question of financing of political parties.
The commission will be examining the means by which political parties should be funded, as well as the provision of funds to political parties from any source, the limits of such funding and the uses to which such funds ought to be or ought not to be put.
It is clear, therefore, that the government agrees that the whole area of the financing of political parties should be examined and that the government should consider whether it is appropriate to modify existing rules and to introduce new regulations, as well as any other changes which may be appropriate.
The matter of the laws concerning election of members of the House of Commons and the rules regulating political parties and candidates is, of course, of fundamental concern to members of this House and to the Canadian public.
The importance that the government places on this subject is reflected in the government's decision to establish the commission of inquiry. Referring the matter of electoral reform and party financing to a commission of inquiry is both appropriate and consistent with past practice. In fact, the blueprint for federal election expenses legislation was the 1966 report of the Committee on Election Expenses, better known as the Barbeau committee.
The chief electoral officer in his annual report tabled April 17, 1989 stated: "I believe that the conduct of a study of the type undertaken by the Barbeau committee would be very useful now in charting future courses of action and that such a study would be best conducted before major amendments are considered to the election expenses provision of our legislation".
The government is committed to changes being made to Canada's electoral laws, to make improvements to those laws, to maintain the integrity of our political system and to make voting easier and more accessible to Canadians. The commission which has been established will be reviewing the existing system and suggesting improvements which can be made.
I thank the hon. member for his interest in this area and I close by indicating that the government looks forward to receiving the recommendations of the Lortie commission.

We know of course that leadership campaigns are very costly. When some people start talking to me about running a national leadership campaign for $80,000, and when I look at the travel expenditures of individual MPs in the Public Accounts listed at the end of the year a number of whom have airline ticket expenditures which exceed $80,000, then I begin to ask myself just how logical is it for any one candidate to pretend that he or she could travel the whole country and not spend any more than $80,000 when for only one Member of Parliament, travelling with no staff or anything during a year that is the amount that one spends?
Obviously a leadership campaign that lasts half a year, assuming that the candidate was going no further than he or she normally goes during a regular off year, if I can put it that way, a year in which there is not a leadership campaign, well half of that amount would be spent anyway just on travelling. Obviously it costs a lot more
December 4, 1989

than $80,000 if you happen to be a member of a national party with seats ranging from Newfoundland to Vancouver Quadra. It is indeed a very expensive proposition.
That being said, I am in favour of looking at this issue in the way that our colleague has suggested. I find it ironic for instance and perhaps sad to see that the laws at the present time are set up in such a way that contributions made to individual candidates for the leadership are not always fully disclosed. We all know of course that a party mechanism can be set up in order to ask various candidates to provide that information at the present time. Will it in fact happen remains to be seen in any political party. One has to remember that if funds are given to a political party, there is no way of knowing how much money actual riding associations collect at the present time.
For instance, if I or any other member is holding a fund raiser for our own constituency association of our political party, and we do that right now, sending the money to the central party for the purposes of receipting and then those funds going back to a riding association, which is the proper way of receiving those contributions, there is no way that the average person can find out which riding association benefited from these funds.
In my previous incarnation as a legislator in the Ontario legislature, the electoral laws in the province of Ontario provided .that each riding association had to make an annual declaration of funds that it received. When I was a provincial member it was easy for any citizen to find out what contributions my association had received during the year. Now that I am a federal member, there is no structure other than asking the riding association if it will volunteer that information, which we do of course in my association. There is no obligation to do that at the present time.
It would be a good idea for us to look at the implications of setting up systems like those so that we know how much not only leadership candidates are getting, but how much riding associations have in the bank, each constituency association of each party in Canada. I think that that should be public information. Right now it is not.
I think we should be able to find out that information in order to modernize the electoral financing laws that we have now. I suspect that most, hopefully all, of us are in a position where there is nothing that we want to hide

Mr. Speaker, I had not originally intended to take part in the debate but I think after hearing a point that my colleague from Comox-Albemi made earlier in his initial presentation, I wanted the opportunity to rise briefly to embellish what I think is a very critical argument in support of my colleague's motion here today in the House.

I want to call this the "kingmaker" factor, or the "queenmaker" factor. There does seem to be in some leadership contests a critical need for a full disclosure of political contributions to those leadership campaigns. I want to go back to the point that my colleague had made earlier in his presentation when he discussed the leadership campaign of the Social Credit Party in 1986 in British Columbia.
To refresh everyone's memory, at that time then Premier Bill Bennett had stepped down from the leadership while he was still premier and had opened up the opportunity for a leadership contest for the party which essentially was paramount to the premiership of the province.
During that time there was a number of very influential business persons in British Columbia who got together and formed what was called the "Golden Twenty" club, a very influential corporate elite of B.C., getting together to basically hold court, and to call before them the corporate elite of British Columbia all the leadership hopefuls of the Social Credit Party to listen to their presentations as to why they should be anointed with not only the leadership of the party but the premiership of the province of British Columbia. Those 20 individuals, essentially, held the power in determining the outcome of that leadership convention that was held later on that year. Those 20 veiy influential individuals basically made the decision for the people of British Columbia, if you can believe it, as to who would be their next premier and which horse they would financially back in that leadership contest.
The concept of democracy, I suggest, went right out the window with that. The premier was anointed. The premier of British Columbia was anointed clearly by that inner sanctum of corporate elite. I suggest that this situation that happened in B.C. a few years ago would never have happened and could never have happened if the regulations had been entrenched in legislation that would force political parties to make public the corporation donations, financial donations, to the various leadership campaigns. There is simply no reason, no
rationale, and certainly no argument in terms of democratic process, that this be allowed to take place.
Going back again, it was very clear that the premiership of the province of British Columbia was up for sale during 1986 and was clearly influenced by a very small handful of very influential, very powerful individuals who made the decision as to which horse they would back financially. I do not think that that is in the interests of any province and certainly not in the interests of Canada as a whole, or, in fact, any democracy when that kind of activity takes place. I think the legislation that is proposed through the motion would avert that kind of situation from happening in the future and that is why I am going to be supporting this motion today.
