speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the House knows, on November 30, the U.S. Congress passed amendments to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Act that impose re-
December 4, 1989

strictions on the size of lobsters that can be sold in the United States. Specifically, no lobsters smaller than the designated U.S. body size of 8.1 centimetres will be allowed for sale. They call this conservation in the States.
We in Canada have had a size limit for lobsters for years. As long as I can remember, there has been a one pound lobster. In Canada there are seasons. It is only open for six months in South West Nova.
There are no limits on traps, no limits on entry in the United States, or on who can catch lobster. We in Canada have had a good conservation policy that has worked well. There have been plenty of one pound lobsters.
If and when President Bush signs this legislation into law, about 10 per cent of Nova Scotia's $130 million live lobster business may be seriously harmed. As Ron Bulmer, president of the Fisheries Council of Canada put it: "If you can't send $30 million worth of live lobster into the United States, where are you going to find a home for it"?
I first raised this issue in the House on October 18.1 asked the hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans what specific actions his government had in mind to prevent these regulations from coming into effect. We know now that whatever actions the government did undertake were of no avail.
Last week, on the eve of his trip to Washington to visit President Bush, I raised this issue with the Prime Minister. I asked him then to assure the House that he would ask the President to veto the new legislation.
Neither the minister nor the Prime Minister have seen fit to let us know exactly what impact Canadian protests are having on the Americans. At least the only clear evidence is that Congress passed the law anyway.
Since the Prime Minister has clearly failed to use his friendship with the President to any positive advantage on this issue, I think we deserve to know precisely when the government will take more concrete action, specifically through the free trade agreement, to eliminate this offensive, trade restricting law.
Canadians are especially interested to know the government's plan in light of the recent free trade panel decision on our salmon and herring conservation pro-
Adjoumment Debate
gram on the west coast. If that program were a restrictive trade practice then surely the dispute settlement panel would look upon the new lobster size regulations the same way.
This government has failed the fishery, both on the west coast and on the east coast. The Minister of Fisheries has been failing it as far as groundfish management and is now doing it in the very lucrative fishery of the lobster. The Minister of Fisheries and Oceans did say that he felt the new regulations "would violate the principle of the free trade agreement". If he is being sincere, and if the government is serious about making sure that the free trade agreement is applied equitably, then we want to see action to back up these words.
It is a weak defence to say that we must wait and see what the President does before taking action since we know that the lobster regulations were attached as a rider to a large piece of legislation which the President cannot veto without throwing out the whole law. So it is unlikely that the President will do anything. Yet we have seen no action nor protest whatever from this government as to the lobster regulations in the States that were in that bill. We must be moving more quickly for a quick reference to the dispute settlement panel because the livelihood of some 6,700 Nova Scotia lobstermen and more from other Atlantic provinces is in jeopardy. If left unchallenged, the new regulations would seriously affect and continue to drive down lobster prices.
If there is anything we need in the Atlantic fishery, it is price stability. Fish prices have been fluctuating wildly this fall. The price of cod on the Portland auction, for example, fell from $1 a pound to 40 cents a pound in the space of one week in October, and that was our cod being caught off the Georges Bank by American fishermen, not Canadian fishermen.
If only as a bid to maintain price stability, we should work strongly to roll back these new regulations, not only for price stability, but because this is offensive legislation. It violates the free trade agreement. It shows that a senator from Maine was able to bring in, without any compassion at all a piece of legislation that will affect the lobster industry, in southern Nova Scotia and all of Nova Scotia without the Prime Minister knowing, having been assured by the President on Labour Day weekend that he would be told that there would be discussions. There have been no discussions with officials.

December 4, 1989
Adjournment Debate
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that it is another example of the Minister of Fisheries' lack of attention to the east coast. It is another example of how the free trade agreement is affecting one small area in the fishery. I do not want to talk about farm stabilization boards or anything like that at this time.
You will have to admit that this legislation in the United States is offensive, Mr. Speaker. The government opposite has done nothing to oppose it. We are going to be faced with a lowering of prices that will be very hard to take.

Mr. Speaker, my address this evening pertains to a question I asked the Minister of National Defence on September 29. The question essentially was with respect to the socioeconomic and the military impact studies that were done in relation to the announced closing of Canadian Forces Base Summerside.

The United States expressed concern over the scope of the new landing regime and we undertook to discuss the new measures with it prior to implementation. During discussions with the United States, we explained the operation of our proposed landing system and that our view was that the system was GATT and FTA consistent.
The United States disagreed with our analysis and claimed that our landing requirement was trade-restrictive. Following further consultations, both parties agreed to submit the dispute to a free trade agreement chapter 18 panel.
The panel proceedings occurred during the summer months and its final report was received on October 16. The panel upheld Canada's sovereign right to conserve and manage the salmon and herring stocks on the west coast. The panel agreed that Canada could establish a landing requirement for salmon and herring but that the present requirements suffered from "overbreadth" in that it applied to 100 per cent of the stocks. However, the
The minister's response was limited by time. The Speaker had to move on, away from Question Period. I thought that I would like to examine some of the factors that were involved, looking at the military impact first. I want you to bear in mind, Sir, that it is not my purpose this evening to do anything with respect to the decision, other than to look at the impact study that I believe should have been done and some of the factors that certainly come to my mind with respect to this decision.
To begin with, looking at the military impact, I would remind the House that in Summerside, there are essentially a couple of main functions, one of which is 413 Search and Rescue Squadron consisting of three Buffalo helicopters and three Labrador aircraft.
Also there are two squadrons, MR-880 Squadron which essentially is a tracker or reconnaissance squadron, and 420 Air Reserve Squadron. The Air Reserve Squadron in fact is twin with the MRR Squadron and



consists of air reservists who fly on their own time to contribute to the defence of the country.
Looking at the decision itself, the impact on the expenditure for the military was almost minuscule. It was one-half of 1 per cent. One wonders really what savings were achieved through that. I understand the difficulty of trying to match infrastructure and national defence with the present size of the force. There is a problem there.
Specifically I am zeroing in on the military impact in Summerside. These tracker aircraft were designed for operation strictly at sea. They were aircraft that flew off an aircraft carrier so that the whole construction of the aircraft is such that they are well suited to do operations at sea.
Their air frame itself, I am told, will be good until the year 2015. What we were looking at was the decision to re-engine them. The decision was made that they would not be re-engined. Therefore there will be no tracker. What we have lost is a capability gap. This is a capability gap of a medium range patrol aircraft in Canada that is organized, manned, controlled and run by the military.
The impact of that was such that a comment was made by the commander of the maritime air group, the change of command, on August 11, 1989. He said that he needed 48 to 60 medium range patrol aircraft to give Canada the ability to patrol its coastal waters. In his view he said that the medium range patrol aircraft was of the highest priority today in the maritime air group.
I would like to talk about this loss of capability added to the relocation of the search and rescue squadron 413 from Summerside to Greenwood. It is a fact that Summerside is strategically located, and I am making reference now to the Cross report of 1982 which was done as a result of a serious search and rescue incident off the east coast of Newfoundland, in Gabriela in 1976, and another serious and tragic incident off Prince Rupert on Christmas Day, 1979.
DND did a study and the Cross report among many other things indicated that Summerside was the most optimum location for search and rescue in the search and rescue region on the Atlantic coast. I am now talking
Adjournment Debate
about an area that is about two million square miles. The strategic location for a search and rescue squadron on which lives are dependent is a very important aspect.
Members who have been close to this in the House are very familiar with the study that was done by Major Gary Naylor and Lieutenant-Colonel Hopping. Major Naylor worked for me directly as a major when I was chief of staff of operations in maritime command. I can certainly attest to his professionalism and his total expertise in search and rescue. Therefore, if Major Naylor indicates that there is a problem and the location in Greenwood is not as optimum or as many lives would not be saved as would be if this were in Summerside, surely it is a serious military impact. I believe this should have been brought forth more to the Canadian public.
As far as the socioeconomic impact is concerned, I do not have to remind this House that we are looking at 1,300 jobs on the base, around 1,300 jobs in the community. The community size is 8,000 people. I am told by the experts in the business that this has the impact of 100,000 jobs in the metropolitan Toronto area. Were that to happen, I can assure you that there would be many members on both sides of this House asking for a military impact study, a socioeconomic impact study and every other kind of an impact study which has not yet been fully disclosed to the House.
I am going to close by mentioning the wind up of the Minister of National Defence in response to my question. I know the Minister of National Defence, probably because he ran out of time, did not mean what he said and would have liked to have added to it if he had not run out of time.
In reference to the devastating socioeconomic impact on the Summerside area, the minister said that we did not identify replacement opportunities or replacement economic activity and that. This is not the responsibility of the Department of National Defence. Well, no question, this may not be the responsibility of the Department of National Defence. But I believe it is very safe to say that it is the responsibility of the government to find something to replace that tremendous gap that is going to be there in 1991, 1992 or 1993, whenever that base is closed.

December 4, 1989
Adjournment Debate
I believe the Canadian public, certainly the people of Summerside, the people of Atlantic Canada, the people on both sides of the House and everybody else needs to know what the impact of this is going to be.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while no specific study was undertaken on the impact of the reductions and closures, a costing methodology was used to determine the projected savings of the base reduction and closure. This methodology examined such items as the impact of the reduction or closure of bases in the past on operational support, personnel and major equipment and facilities. In addition, experience gained through Cadin-Pinetree closures made it possible to keep any likely impact to a minimum.
To this end, DND and Employment and Immigration Canada are co-operating closely and, as the hon. member knows, local committees have been established to provide assistance to affected employees.
The hon. member should also be aware, and I am sure he is, that DND is co-operating fully with other agencies of the federal and provincial governments in their endeavours to identify suitable re-use for any facilities on bases to be closed or any surplus facilities on bases being reduced.
With regard to specific studies on the impact on military effectiveness as a result of closures or reductions, I am surprised that the hon. member would ask such a question. Indeed, the hon. member had a long and distinguished naval career and I am certain that he knows that every decision taken by the Department of National Defence is based on this very essential consideration.
For some time, Canada has maintained military installations in excess of the requirement of the current size of the Canadian Forces. The aim, therefore, is to achieve more efficient use of resources through the reduction or elimination of sites which no longer fill an operational need. I would add that this will not reduce our military effectiveness.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to again get involved in the question that I asked of the Minister of Transport on Monday, November 21, as it relates to VIA Rail and, more
specifically, the elimination of the VIA Rail passenger route called The Canadian.
On that particular day, the question I raised was basically a question as it related to the figures I had been given by the VIA people in Winnipeg. Those particular figures that I suggested to the minister showed some very interesting and puzzling scenarios for the people of northwestern Ontario and, more important, for the people who ride on The Canadian.
Again I would like to relate those numbers to the government opposite and to the people of Canada to show that there seems to be some difficulty in the rationale put forward by the government which is, as the Prime Minister has said: "Use it or lose it".
I explained to the minister on that particular day that eight months is not a short period of time. The minister at the time said: "Well, if you want to put two weeks together or a month together, anybody can play with numbers". Eight months is a long period of time on a particular VIA run which, in essence, shows whether someone is using a particular route or not.
Just for the record, I would like to state the figures. The over-all ridership on The Canadian for that period of time was 93 per cent which is in all estimates pretty well full capacity. It has also been told to us by the people in VIA that it is considered that by 1993 they will be over capacity and will have to do something about that particular run and in essence put on more cars.
The Montreal to Vancouver train carried over 34,800 passengers, a load factor of 98.8 per cent. Travelling from the west to Montreal, the Vancouver train carried over
33,000	passengers, with a load factor of 98 per cent. In northwestern Ontario, the Toronto to Sudbury train which connects with the Montreal train carried over 8,580 passengers which is 85 per cent capacity while the Sudbury to Toronto train carried over 8,890 passengers which is 93.3 per cent capacity.
The reason I raised the question in the House of Commons was because of the scenario that the government has put forward on numerous occasions, that the reason these particular runs were eliminated was that nobody was riding them. As an ex-railroader I had a little difficulty with that particular scenario because I happen to know a lot about trains just in common practice. I went and did a little checking and found out from people
December 4, 1989

who I know in the industry that lo and behold, this particular run is the most efficient run in all of Canada.
I was a little bit at a loss for words to understand what the scenario was. Then I found out something very interesting that happened during the cuts to VIA. Under the revamped network, VIA trains will travel on CN tracks 96 per cent of the time and on Canadian Pacific routes 4 per cent of the time in comparison to the 77 per cent and 23 per cent under the previous arrangements.
There has been a switch to running on CP tracks which happen to be the ones that are the majority of the track that The Canadian runs on in the southern routes to the northern CN route which also has a lack of people riding on these trains for one particular reason. It is not that people do not want to. It is just that in the northern route, fewer people live there. It makes me wonder what the scenario really is.
There are two reasons obviously. One is that if fewer people use the 50 per cent that is left, then they can justify getting rid of it and the other factor is that if they take a look at the amount of money that is paid to CN as far as rental of track per year, and if they took that away, CN would be in the hole. It would not be making a profit so there are two reasons why Mr. Lawless decided that this would be the best scenario for VIA.
I brought this matter up today because I wanted to give the government the opportunity to explain to me and Canadians, and particularly the people in northwestern Ontario, what its rationale really was for eliminating this very important piece of trackage. The figures show that there is no necessity.
There has been no environmental impact study. Again, I brought that up at a meeting of the environment committee and I asked environment officials if they could tell me exactly what the level of C02 emissions would be once that roughly one million passengers would be using vehicles when the cuts went into effect. Basically they said: "We don't know that number," whereas the minister stood in his place in this House and said that the environmental impact would be negligible. If you do not know what the upper limit is as far as C02 emissions are concerned, how can you say that 1 million cars more is negligible? In essence, the people in the Ministry of the
Adjournment Debate
Environment told me that that is an unknown factor, therefore, we cannot really tell you that answer.
I think that the government opposite has pulled a fast one on the Canadian people and has not shown the impact on the environment that this will have. Therefore, I think it is important that the government take a look at this particular route that I am talking about today which is The Canadian because it did not even look at options to improve the run. For example, in the summer, it is so full you cannot get on.
I suggest that if you want to eliminate the subsidy on a route like that, put more cars on in the summer when the tourism season is at its peak instead of just cutting the route completely and throwing hundreds of people out of a job, as well as affecting the tourism trade in an area of northern Ontario which I know for a fact foreigners come to on a regular basis by train because of its beauty and the magnitude of that particular geographical area.
In conclusion, I ask the parliamentary secretary to explain to me and to northwestern Ontarians and people who had The Canadian and no longer have it, what the rationale really is behind this particular cut-back to VIA and to what we call The Canadian.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ross Belsher (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: SITTING RESUMED The House resumed at 5.55 p.m.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River for again raising this very important subject not only to his area, but also to people across the prairie provinces as well.
I might say to the hon. member that the decision to discontinue the passenger service provided by the western transcontinental train, or better known as The Canadian, was taken because the country cannot continue to provide the large subsidies required to operate the total service of VIA Rail and so there had to be cuts made within the VIA Rail system.
In 1988, The Canadian service carried approximately
545.000	passengers and had a load factor of some 70 per cent. The cost for this service exceeded revenues by $109 million. That was in 1988. The subsidy for each passenger who travelled on The Canadian was $199. Between January and October of this year The Canadian carried
466.000	passengers, an increase of 16 per cent over the ridership for the same period of the year before. The load factor for the first 10 months of this year was increased to 83.5 per cent.
It is true that during the summer months demands for space on these trains has exceeded supply, which the hon. member alluded to in his previous remarks. This is

Adjournment Debate
not a new situation. It has occurred in varying degrees for a number of years. However, it is not economically feasible to spend millions of dollars for passenger cars which are only used during the summer.
Even with the increased level of ridership, the service will require a subsidy in excess of $100 million for 1989. On the basis of this financial reality, the government stands by its decision to discontinue The Canadian. While the service over the route followed by The Canadian between Toronto and Vancouver via Thunder Bay and Calgary will be discontinued, transcontinental
service will continue to be provided as stated in the October 4, 1989 announcement. The government has decided that a tri-weekly service will operate between Toronto and Vancouver via Sioux Lookout and Edmonton.
